That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense you'd want a break from it all. Wanting to disappear for a while, not forever, often comes from feeling overloaded and like there's no space to just breathe. It’s exhausting to carry responsibilities constantly without a pause.

If you’re open to sharing, what’s feeling heaviest right now? Sometimes naming even one or two of those responsibilities out loud can make them feel a little less like one giant wall.

When the urge to just get away comes up, it can help to give yourself tiny, realistic pockets of “away” in the moment, even if it’s just for a few minutes:
* Step outside, change rooms, or put your phone on do not disturb for a short stretch
* Do one small thing that’s just for you, not for anyone else, like a song you love, a warm shower, or stepping away to stretch
* Write down what’s on your mind without editing it, then set it aside so it doesn’t have to loop in your head
* Notice when you’re running on empty and give yourself permission to say no or postpone one non-urgent thing

You deserve rest and space, not just when everything is done. If you have someone you trust, even just letting them know “I’m feeling overwhelmed and need a bit of space” can lighten the load a little.

You don’t have to figure all of this out alone. Is there one small part of this that feels most urgent to talk through, or one kind of break that would feel most restorative right now?

The fact that it ends doesn’t necessarily cancel out the fact that it matters *while it’s happening*. A song is still worth listening to even though it stops. That doesn’t make the stopping less true, but it can make the listening still worth it.

That feeling of missing out while you're working so hard to provide is incredibly painful, and it's understandable you'd be carrying guilt about it. Many parents feel this tension between needing to work and wanting to be present for the moments that matter with their kids. You're not alone in that.

It makes sense you’d feel like you’re failing when you’re missing things — school events, bedtime stories, just the everyday in-between moments that add up. It can be hard to separate the reality of what you’re doing for your family from the story your mind tells you about what a "good parent" should be doing.

If you’re open to reflecting a bit, I'm curious what "missing everything" looks like for you day-to-day. Is it the big milestones, the daily connection, or a mix of both? And when that feeling of failing comes up, what do you notice in your body and thoughts in that moment?

You’re in a tough spot where work demands and parenting demands are both real and both important. Some parents find it helps to gently shift from "am I present enough?" to "how can I be present in the ways I can right now?" Even small, intentional moments can matter a lot to kids:

* Creating a predictable ritual, even if brief, like a 5-minute check-in at bedtime or a good morning hug, so they feel the connection is reliable
* Sharing a little of what you’re carrying with them in age-appropriate ways, like “I wish I could stay for the game, I’m proud of you and I’m thinking of you while I work”
* Noticing and naming the moments you *do* get to have, even if they’re small, so the good doesn't get erased by the guilt
* Giving yourself the same compassion you’d offer a friend in this situation. Working hard to support your family *is* a form of care for your kids, even if it costs you presence

It can also help to think about what is actually within your control. Are there conversations that feel possible to have — with a partner, family member, or even at work about hours or flexibility? Sometimes just mapping out what’s non-negotiable vs. what might have a little wiggle room can reduce that overwhelmed feeling.

You deserve support too, not just your kids. Is there anyone in your life you feel safe talking to about this guilt and exhaustion, or a space where you can decompress after work so you’re not carrying it all alone?

If these feelings start feeling heavy, persistent, or like they’re getting harder to manage, consider reaching out to a trusted healthcare provider or support person for extra help.

You care deeply about your kids — that care is evident in how much this hurts you. That matters.

*This is general support, not therapy or professional advice.*

The scale is also a very narrow snapshot of what’s happening in your body, and it can be influenced by a lot of things that have nothing to do with fat loss — water retention from hormones, sleep, stress or salty meals, muscle changes from activity, normal daily fluctuations, and even time of day you weigh.

Sometimes when the number doesn’t move, it can help to check in with how you’re feeling overall, not just the scale. * Prioritizing regular, adequate sleep and rest days
* Moving in ways you actually enjoy and can keep up with, rather than only “exercise for weight loss”
* Eating in a way that feels nourishing and satisfying, with regular meals and enough variety
* Noticing stress and emotional cues around food and the scale, and practicing self-compassion when frustration comes up

If you’ve been trying for months and feel stuck or discouraged, it can be really helpful to talk with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian who can get a fuller picture of your health history, habits, and goals with you. It's completely understandable to feel nervous before surgery — it's a big, vulnerable thing to go through, and the fear of "what if I don't wake up" is a very common worry. You're not alone in feeling this way.

I'm an AI, not a medical professional, so I can't speak to the safety of your specific procedure or anesthesia. Only your surgical and anesthesia team, who know your health history and the details of your surgery, can answer questions about risks and safety for you. If this fear is weighing on you tonight, it's absolutely appropriate to call your care team or the pre-op nurse line. They would much rather answer your concerns now than have you go in feeling scared and alone with them.

If you are able to talk to them before tomorrow, many people find it helps to write down their questions ahead of time, for example:
* Who will be monitoring me during surgery and anesthesia?
* What is the plan for my safety during and after the procedure?
* What should I expect to feel when I wake up in recovery?
* Who can I contact tonight if my anxiety spikes?

You can also ask to speak with an anesthesiologist before the day of surgery. They are specifically trained in keeping patients safe during anesthesia and are used to talking through these exact fears.

For tonight, some gentle coping strategies that many people find helpful with pre-surgery anxiety:

* **Ground your body.** Slow, paced breathing can help calm the nervous system. Try inhaling for 4 counts, holding for 1-2, and exhaling for 6 counts, repeating a few times.
* **Limit "what if" spirals.** When the fear pops up, try naming it: "I'm having the thought that I won't wake up." Then redirect to something concrete and present, like the feel of your blanket, the sound in the room, or one thing you're looking forward to after recovery.
* **Get support.** If you have someone you trust, let them know you're nervous. Ask them to be with you before you go in, or to be the person who talks to the team and helps you remember information.
* **Prepare practically.** Pack your bag, set out comfortable clothes, and follow your pre-op instructions exactly. Having practical things handled can reduce a little of the mental load.

It's normal for anxiety to be higher the night before. If you find the fear is becoming overwhelming, interfering with sleep, or turning into panic, please reach out to your care team, primary doctor, or a mental health professional for support.

If you want, you can tell me a bit about what kind of support would feel most helpful right now — like help writing questions for your doctor, or calming exercises for tonight — and I can help with that.

*This is general support information, not medical advice. For any concerns about your surgery, anesthesia, or health, please contact your medical team directly.*

That sounds exhausting. Feeling bored and like you're stuck on repeat can be really draining, especially when it starts to feel like nothing changes day to day.

You're not alone in feeling that way — a lot of people hit that flat, monotonous stretch where work/school, home, sleep, repeat starts to blur together. It doesn't mean you're doing something wrong, it often means your brain is craving a little more stimulation, meaning, or novelty than it's getting right now.

If you're open to it, I'm curious: what does "on repeat" look like for you lately? Is it the same routine, same thoughts, same people, or more like nothing feels exciting or new anymore?

Sometimes when that feeling shows up, it helps to experiment with tiny disruptions rather than big overhauls. Not to "fix" boredom, just to notice what shifts it even a little:

* **Change the sensory input.** Take a different route home, listen to a genre you never touch, cook with one new ingredient, change your desk setup. Novelty doesn't have to be huge to register.
* **Add a 10-minute curiosity window.** Pick something completely low-stakes and just explore it for 10 minutes — a random Wikipedia rabbit hole, a free museum virtual tour, a YouTube tutorial on something weird. The goal isn't productivity, it's just breaking the loop.
* **Track the flat spots.** For a couple days, jot down when the boredom/repeat feeling spikes. Is it mornings, after work, on weekends? Patterns can show you where a small tweak might help most.
* **Reconnect with one small thing you used to like.** Not the "big passion" pressure, just something that used to be easy and pleasant, even if it's just doodling, walking without headphones, or texting one person you miss.

If this feeling has been hanging around for a while and it's starting to bleed into things like sleep, appetite, motivation, or mood, it can be worth talking to someone you trust or a mental health professional. You deserve support for that, not just pushing through it.

Does that resonate with what you're experiencing? Or is it more like feeling invisible, unseen, or like you don't belong in your own story?

* When do you notice that feeling most strongly? Is it at certain times of day, around certain people, or after certain things happen?

* Have there been moments, even brief ones, when you felt more present or connected to yourself? What was different then?

You don't have to answer any of that if it's too much right now. Just know that feeling detached or unseen doesn't mean you're broken or alone in feeling this way.

* Grounding in the senses, like naming 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, 1 you can taste. It can help bring attention back to the present moment.
* Writing down what you're experiencing without editing it, even just a few lines, to get it out of your head and onto paper.
* Small acts of connection with one person you trust, even a short text saying "I'm having a hard time today" if that feels possible.
* Treating yourself with the same kindness you'd offer a friend who said this to you.

If this sense of disconnection is persistent, getting worse, or making it hard to function day to day, talking to a mental health professional or a trusted medical provider can be a supportive next step. You deserve support for this.

Feeling guilty for being happy when there is so much pain in the world is a really human response, and you’re not alone in experiencing it. Many people find themselves caught between wanting to stay connected to suffering and also wanting to allow themselves moments of joy, rest, or lightness. Those two things can feel like they’re in conflict, even though they don’t have to be.

It makes sense that this guilt comes up. When you care about others and are aware of injustice, loss, or hardship, it can feel selfish or wrong to experience happiness. Sometimes people describe this as a kind of empathic distress — the heart wants to stay open to what’s hurting, and then feels uncomfortable when it also feels relief, laughter, or contentment.

It’s important to know that feeling happy does not mean you don’t care, and it doesn’t erase the reality of what’s happening in the world. Joy and sorrow can coexist. Allowing yourself moments of peace can actually help you stay engaged with the world over time, rather than burning out.

If this guilt is coming up for you a lot, it can help to gently explore it with yourself:

* What does the guilt tell you about your values? Often it signals that compassion and solidarity matter to you.
* Is there a specific situation or news story that’s been sitting with you? Sometimes naming what’s weighing on you makes the feeling less vague and overwhelming.
* What does “being happy” look like for you right now? Is it small everyday moments, or a sense that you should be doing more? There’s a difference between enjoying a moment and ignoring the world.

Some gentle ways people find relief from this kind of guilt:

* Practice self-compassion. Remind yourself that you are allowed to be a whole person who can hold both care for others and care for yourself. You don’t have to earn rest.
* Give your attention boundaries. Constant exposure to distressing news can make it hard to feel any ease. Choosing intentional times to check in, and times to step away, can protect your capacity to care.
* Allow both feelings to exist. You can acknowledge “I’m grateful for this good moment, and I’m also heartbroken about what’s happening elsewhere.” Both can be true.
* Channel concern in a way that feels sustainable, if you want to. For some people that’s small, values-aligned actions; for others it’s supporting others, learning, donating, or advocating. The key is choosing something that feels meaningful rather than driven by guilt alone.
* Notice self-criticism. Try speaking to yourself the way you would to a friend who told you they felt guilty for laughing at a joke while bad things are happening in the world.

If you notice this guilt is persistent, taking up a lot of mental space, or making it hard to enjoy things you normally find meaningful, it can be helpful to talk it through with someone you trust or a mental health professional. You deserve support in navigating these conflicting feelings without having to push them away.

If you feel comfortable sharing, what kinds of moments of happiness are you feeling guilty about, and what is weighing on you most right now? I’m here to listen.

Feeling insecure about your art hurts, and it makes sense that you're carrying that right now. When you look at other people's work and feel like yours just doesn't measure up, it can be really lonely and discouraging, especially if making art matters a lot to you.

It's really common for artists to get stuck in that comparison loop. What you see online or in person is usually a highlight reel — finished pieces, best angles, the work people choose to show — not the messy drafts, the abandoned sketches, the days they felt stuck or frustrated. It's easy for your own in-process, private work to feel "less than" next to that.

If you're open to reflecting a bit, I'm curious: what makes you feel like your art isn't as good right now? Is there a specific piece, a recent feedback moment, or just scrolling and comparing that's been loud lately? And when you say "as good as everyone else's," what does "good" mean to you in that moment — technical skill, originality, how people react to it?

You don't have to earn permission to keep making. Art isn't a ranking, and your worth as an artist isn't determined by how your work stacks up against someone else's. Growth in art tends to be slow and non-linear, and insecurity often shows up most when you actually care deeply and are pushing yourself.

If this feeling is weighing on you, some gentle things people find helpful in those moments:

* **Separate process from product.** Notice one thing you learned or enjoyed in the act of making, even if the outcome feels imperfect. What was one moment you were curious or absorbed in?
* **Limit comparison windows.** If scrolling is feeding the insecurity, it can help to set a time boundary for it, and intentionally go back to your own work or references you love for inspiration, not evaluation.
* **Get specific and kind with yourself.** Instead of "it's not good," try asking "what do I like about this part?" and "what do I want to explore next time?" That shifts from judgment to direction.
* **Share with a safe person.** One trusted friend, mentor, or fellow artist who can give feedback on your intentions, not just the finish, can be a counterbalance to the inner critic.

You deserve space to make art without constantly measuring it against others. What would it feel like to give yourself a little more room to just practice and explore for a while, without the grade?

I'm here to listen if you want to talk more about what's been triggering this, or about your work itself.

That sounds really frightening, and it makes sense you’re still shaking after waking up from a nightmare. Your body is still in that high-alert state, even though you’re safe in bed now.

Give yourself a moment to come back to the present. You don’t have to process the dream right now if you don’t want to.

If it feels okay, here are a few gentle things you can try to help your nervous system settle:

* **Ground through your senses.** Look around the room and quietly name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can feel — like the texture of your blanket or the floor under your feet, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste. This can help anchor you back in the here-and-now.
* **Slow your breathing.** Try a gentle rhythm if it feels comfortable: inhale slowly through your nose for about 4 counts, and exhale slowly through your mouth for about 6 counts. You don’t have to do it perfectly, just a few slow breaths can signal to your body that the danger has passed.
* **Care for your body.** Sit up slowly, place both feet on the floor, wrap yourself in a blanket or hold something warm and comforting. Sip some water if you’re able. Moving gently, like stretching your arms overhead or shaking out your hands, can help release some of that leftover tension.
* **Create a little buffer before sleep.** If you’re not ready to go back to sleep right away, try a calming activity instead of scrolling or replaying the nightmare — dim lights, listen to soft sounds, read something neutral, or write a few lines about how you feel now to get it out of your head.

Nightmares can leave a strong imprint, especially in the first minutes after waking. It’s okay if your thoughts feel jumbled or your heart is still racing.

If you want, you can tell me a little about what you’re feeling in this moment, or what would feel most supportive right now. If nightmares like this are happening often or are starting to affect your sleep and daytime wellbeing, talking to a trusted person or a mental health professional can be really helpful.

It makes sense that you're worried — caring about a friend and feeling unsure how to help can be really stressful and lonely. You don't have to fix everything for them to be supportive, and just being a steady, caring presence matters a lot.

Here are some ways you can show up for them while also protecting your own wellbeing:

**Start with connection, not solutions**
* Let them know you've noticed and you care. Something simple like, "I've missed you lately" or "I've noticed you seem different/stressed, and I'm here if you want to talk" can open the door without putting them on the spot.
* Listen more than you advise. Try reflecting back what you hear: "It sounds like you've been going through a lot lately." Validation — "That makes sense you'd feel exhausted" — often helps more than trying to find the right words of advice.
* Ask open, gentle questions and follow their lead. "How have you been feeling about things?" is better than "Are you okay?" which can feel too big to answer. Let them decide how much to share.

**Be patient and consistent**
* People often pull away when they're struggling. It can help to keep showing up in low-pressure ways — a text, sending a meme, inviting them for a walk — so they know you're there even if they don't talk right away.
* Avoid minimizing or comparing experiences, even if you mean well. Phrases like "It could be worse" or "Just cheer up" can make someone feel unheard. Try staying curious instead: "I can't imagine exactly how that feels, but I want to understand."

**Support them in getting more help if needed**
* If they open up about feeling overwhelmed, hopeless, or like they can't cope, you can gently encourage professional support: "You deserve support for this, have you thought about talking to a counselor or doctor?"
* You can offer practical help with that step if they want it, like helping them find resources or sitting with them while they make a call. It's okay to say you can't be their therapist, and that's normal.
* If you ever become worried about their safety — for example they talk about harming themselves, not wanting to be alive, or you notice a sudden change in behavior — take it seriously. Encourage them to reach out for immediate help, and don't keep it a secret. In the US, you can call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. If you believe someone is in immediate danger, call emergency services, 911.

**Take care of your own boundaries**
* Supporting a friend can be emotionally draining. Check in with yourself about what you can realistically offer.
* It's okay to set limits: "I care about you a lot and I want to be there, and I also need to take care of myself tonight."
* Talk to someone you trust about your own worries — a friend, family member, or counselor — so you're not carrying this alone.

You don't need to have the perfect words or the perfect plan. Often the most helpful thing is simply letting your friend know they aren't alone and that you’re willing to listen without judgment.

If you feel comfortable sharing, what changes have you been noticing in them? I can help you think through how to approach a specific situation.

*This is general support information, not professional mental health advice. If you or your friend are in crisis or need immediate help, please contact a crisis helpline in your country or emergency services.*

That sounds really overwhelming, and it makes sense you want to hide out right now. Having to witness a huge fight between your parents can leave you feeling scared, tense, or just numb, and needing space to get away from it is a completely understandable reaction.

You don't have to process everything in this moment. If you can, just focus on getting through the next few minutes safely and calmly.

If you feel safe where you are, you could try giving your nervous system a little reset:
* **Ground yourself.** Try slow breathing: inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 6. Do that a few times. Or name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, 1 you can taste.
* **Create a small calm corner.** Put on low music or a white noise/rain sound, dim the lights, wrap up in a blanket, and do something that is just for you for 10 minutes — a game, a sketch, a shower, journaling a few lines about what you're feeling without needing to make sense of it.
* **Contain the thoughts.** It can help to write down what you’re hearing and what you’re feeling in a notes app or paper, and then literally put it aside. You don’t have to fix it right now.

You shouldn’t have to be the mediator or the peacekeeper in the middle of their fight. It’s okay to protect your own space while they work things out.

When things calm down, it can help to check in with yourself: What do you need after an episode like this? Some people find it helpful to have a plan, like having a door you can close, headphones ready, or a trusted person you can text "it's loud at home" to.

If you ever feel unsafe — like you’re afraid someone might get hurt, or you feel threatened — please reach out for immediate help. Do you have one person you trust — a friend, relative, school counselor, coach — who knows this is happening and you could talk to when you’re ready? You don’t have to go through this alone.

If you want, you can tell me a little about what you’re feeling right now, or what’s been hardest about these fights. I’m here to listen.

That sounds really overwhelming, and it's completely understandable to feel stressed when you're facing a lot of work and worried you won't be able to finish it. A lot of people hit that point where the to-do list feels bigger than the time they have.

You don't have to figure it all out at once. If you're open to it, it can help to get some of that swirl out of your head and onto paper. A quick brain dump of everything that's on your plate, even the small stuff, can make it feel less vague and scary.

When you're in that overwhelmed state, sometimes just picking a starting point helps more than trying to solve everything:

* **Shrink it down to 3.** Look at your list and ask: If I could only get 3 things done today, what would make the biggest difference? Give yourself permission to let the rest wait until tomorrow.

Feeling like you’re failing at being an adult and can’t keep up with anything is an exhausting place to be. It makes sense that it would leave you discouraged, especially when there’s so much pressure to have it all together — bills, work/school, chores, relationships, health — and it never seems to slow down.

You’re not alone in that feeling. A lot of people hit a point where the to-do list feels endless and the gap between what they think they “should” be handling and what they’re actually able to handle feels huge. That gap can be really painful, and it often says more about unrealistic expectations and being overloaded than it does about you as a person.

If you’re open to it, I’m curious what “can’t keep up” looks like for you right now. Is it more about daily tasks piling up, feeling behind at work or school, the home stuff, or a general sense of mental fog and exhaustion? Sometimes naming the specific areas that feel heaviest can make it a little less overwhelming.

In the meantime, if this feeling is weighing on you, here are some gentle things people find helpful when adulting feels impossible:

**Give yourself a reality check on expectations.** Adulting isn’t one standard. There’s no single timeline for having it “figured out.” Comparing your behind-the-scenes to other people’s highlight reels only makes the gap feel bigger.

**Shrink the task, not the worth.** When everything feels like too much, picking one tiny, doable next step can help break the freeze. Instead of “clean the apartment,” it might be “put three dishes in the sink.” Instead of “catch up on everything,” it might be “choose one thing for today.” Small wins build momentum and give your nervous system a little relief.

**Notice the self-talk.** It’s easy for the inner critic to turn “I’m struggling right now” into “I’m failing.” If you can catch that thought, try offering yourself the same kind of words you’d give a friend: “This is really hard right now, and I’m doing the best I can with what I have.”

**Check in with basics.** Sleep, food, movement, and downtime aren’t luxuries — they’re the infrastructure that makes it possible to function. When you’re running on empty, even simple things feel monumental. If you’ve been neglecting any of those, it’s understandable.

**You don’t have to sort it all out alone.** Is there one person you trust who could know how heavy this feels, even if you don’t ask for solutions? Sometimes just saying “I’m overwhelmed and feel like I’m falling behind” out loud can take some of the pressure off.

If this feeling of falling behind is persistent, getting darker, or starting to interfere with your ability to function day to day, it can be really helpful to talk to a mental health professional or a trusted medical provider. You deserve support that’s tailored to you, not just tips.

How long have you been feeling this way? And is there one area that feels the most urgent to tackle, or does it feel like everything at once?

I’m here to listen if you want to unpack more.

Feeling like a burden to the people around you is a really painful place to be in, and it makes sense that you’d want to reach out about it. That kind of thought can be heavy and lonely, and you deserve support for carrying it.

I’m not a mental health professional, just an AI here to listen. I can’t know your full situation, but I can hear how much weight you’re feeling right now.

Sometimes thoughts like “I’m a burden” show up when we’ve been under a lot of stress, when we’ve been putting other people’s needs first for a long time, or when we’re struggling and worry we’re asking too much. It doesn’t mean it’s true — it means you’re in pain and maybe feeling disconnected from the people you care about.

If you’re open to exploring it a little, I’m curious:
* When did you start noticing this feeling? Is it with specific people or situations?
* What makes you feel like a burden in those moments — is it needing help, reaching out, or something else?

You don’t have to answer that here if you don’t want to. Even naming the feeling out loud can be a first step.

In the meantime, some gentle things people find helpful when they’re stuck in that loop:

* **Check the evidence with compassion.** Our minds often jump to the worst story when we’re hurting. Try noticing one small moment recently where someone stayed, listened, or cared — even if it felt small. That doesn’t erase the pain, but it can balance the harsh inner critic.
* **Talk to one safe person.** It can be scary to say “I’ve been feeling like a burden lately” but often people care more than we expect. You could start small, like “I’ve been having a hard time lately.”
* **Give yourself the same patience you’d give a friend.** If a friend said “I feel like a burden,” you probably wouldn’t agree with them. You could try speaking to yourself in that same kinder tone.
* **Care for your basics.** Sleep, food, movement, and moments of quiet can make those heavy thoughts louder or quieter. Even a 5-minute walk or writing down what’s on your mind can help create a little space.

If these thoughts are getting louder, persistent, or making it hard to function, talking to a mental health professional or a trusted medical provider can be a really important next step. You don’t have to wait until it feels unbearable to deserve support.

If you ever feel unsafe or like you might act on thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out for immediate help. In the US you can call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the US, you can find your country’s helpline at https://findahelpline.com.

* Who will be with me during surgery and who will be the first person to update me and my support person afterward?
* What should I do tonight to prepare, and what should I avoid?
* What signs should I watch for during recovery, and who do I call if I have concerns?

Writing those questions down can make them feel more manageable, and bringing a trusted person with you can help you remember the answers.

results.model_response:
That is so infuriating, and it's completely understandable that you're angry. Having your work taken credit for — especially when it's happened again — feels disrespectful, invisible, and exhausting. Anyone would want to scream.

You deserve to have your contributions seen.

If you need to get the intensity down right now, before you decide what to do next:
* **Give yourself a pause.** Step away from your desk if you can, splash cold water on your hands, or take 5 slow breaths in for 4 counts, out for 6. Anger is valid, but acting on it while you're at peak is when things can backfire.
* **Get it out somewhere safe.** Vent to a trusted friend, write it out in a notes app and don't send it, or say it out loud in your car. You shouldn't have to swallow that feeling.
* **Name what happened factually.** "I built the presentation / wrote the report / solved X on [date] and my boss presented it as theirs in the meeting on [date]." Writing it down helps separate the sting from the facts.

When you're ready to think about what you want to do, you have options and you don't have to pick one today:

* **Document.** Keep a private record of your work: drafts with timestamps, emails, Slack threads, meeting notes where you contributed. That paper trail is power if you decide to push back later.
* **Clarify your goal.** Do you want credit this time, to prevent it happening again, or are you starting to think about leaving? The approach is different for each.
* **If you want to address it directly:** A calm, private conversation can be "I felt really discouraged when the work I did on X was presented without attribution. I'd like my contributions to be acknowledged going forward." Keep it focused on one specific incident and what you need.
* **Find allies.** Is there a teammate who knows the work is yours? A mentor or skip-level manager you trust? Sometimes a witness makes it harder for the behavior to continue unchecked.
* **Check your workplace policies.** Some companies have processes for attribution, feedback, or HR support. You don't have to go to HR immediately, but knowing what exists helps.

How are you feeling right now in this moment — do you just need space to vent about it, or are you wanting to brainstorm how to handle your boss?

I'm here for either.

That makes a lot of sense, and you're definitely not alone in feeling that way. When the future feels unclear, it's very normal for the mind to fill in the gaps with worst-case scenarios and for that to bring up fear, restlessness, or even exhaustion.

Uncertainty is uncomfortable for all of us because we naturally want some sense of predictability and safety. Right now the world can feel especially unpredictable, and it's hard not to take that in personally, even when you just want to know what comes next for you.

If you're open to it, it can help to get a little more specific with yourself about what the fear is pointing to. Sometimes "the future" feels big and scary because it's a bundle of smaller worries. Is it more about work/school, finances, relationships, health, or a general sense that things are changing too fast to keep up with? You don't have to figure it all out, just noticing what comes up first can make it feel less overwhelming.

In the meantime, here are some gentle ways people find a bit of steadiness when uncertainty spikes:

**Ground in the present moment.** When fear about the future takes over, your nervous system can get stuck in "what if". A simple pause can help: plant both feet on the floor, notice 3 things you can see, 2 things you can feel, and 1 thing you can hear. Slow breathing, like inhaling for 4 counts and exhaling for 6, can also signal to your body that you are safe right now.

**Shrink the time horizon.** The future is huge, so try making it smaller. Instead of thinking about "the next 5 years", ask "what's one small, doable thing for today?" That could be drinking water, sending one email, stepping outside for 5 minutes. Small actions create a little sense of agency when the big picture feels foggy.

**Name it without judgment.** It can help to say to yourself, "I'm having the thought that the future is scary and uncertain." Labeling the feeling can create a little distance so it doesn't take up the whole room.

**Limit the worry inputs.** News, social media, and endless scrolling can make uncertainty feel bigger than it is. If you notice those loops making you more anxious, try setting a time boundary for checking in, and intentionally add one thing that feels grounding or nourishing.

**Lean on connection.** Fear often grows in isolation. Talking to someone you trust, even just saying "I've been feeling really anxious about what's ahead," can lighten the load. You don't have to have solutions to deserve support.

If you notice this fear is getting heavier, interfering with sleep, appetite, concentration, or daily life for a while, it can be really helpful to reach out to a mental health professional or a trusted support person. You deserve support while you navigate this.

I am so, so sorry for your loss. Losing a dog is losing a family member, a daily companion, and a whole piece of your life and routine. It makes complete sense that you are crying and feel like you can’t stop right now. Grief doesn’t follow a schedule, and those first hours and days after saying goodbye can feel raw and overwhelming.

Please be gentle with yourself today. Crying is not something you need to stop or “fix” — it’s your heart responding to love and loss. If tears are coming, let them come. You don’t have to be strong or hold it together for anyone right now.

If it feels possible, just try to care for the basics in small, kind ways: sip some water, rest when you can, and give yourself permission to not do anything “productive.” Grief is exhausting.

Some people find it helps in the early days to:

* Give yourself space to remember. Look at photos, hold a favorite toy or collar, or write down a few memories of your dog if and when you feel ready. There is no right way to remember.
* Say their name out loud. Acknowledge them and the bond you shared.
* Reach out to one person you trust, even if it’s just to text “my dog died and I’m not okay.” You don’t have to explain or minimize it.
* If the crying feels unending and you’re worried about your own safety or ability to function, please consider reaching out to a trusted person or a professional for support. You deserve care too.

You loved your dog deeply, and that love doesn’t end with them. I’m here if you want to share their name, a memory, or just have a place to express how hard this is right now.

I’m really sorry you’re going through this.

That sounds really rough. Messing up a big presentation can feel humiliating and leave you replaying it over and over, and it's completely understandable that you're feeling like a failure right now.

One tough moment, even a high-stakes one, doesn't erase everything you've done or what you're capable of. Our brains tend to turn a mistake into a whole identity story — "I failed" becomes "I am a failure" — especially when you're already stressed and putting yourself out there. It makes sense that the feeling is loud right now.

If you're in that spiral right now, it can help to give yourself a little space from the story:

* **Pause the replay.** When the thoughts start looping, try grounding for a minute. Name 3 things you can see, 2 you can feel, and 1 you can hear. It won't fix it, but it can dial down the intensity so you can think more clearly.
* **Get the facts vs. the story.** What actually happened? Maybe you blanked, lost your slides, went over time, etc. That's a specific event. "I'm a total failure" is a judgment about your worth. Try separating them: "I had a bad presentation" is true and painful, "I'm a failure" is an interpretation.
* **Treat yourself like you'd treat a teammate.** If a friend messed up a presentation, you probably wouldn't call them a total failure. You'd likely say "that sucks, presentations are hard." What would you say to them? Can you offer yourself even a fraction of that same kindness?
* **Learn what you can, when you're ready.** Once the initial sting eases, you can pick one small, concrete thing to note for next time if you want to — like practicing the first 60 seconds, having a backup slide, etc. Not to punish yourself, but so the experience can become information instead of just shame.

It might also help to talk it out with someone you trust, or write down what went through your head during and after. Sometimes getting it out of your head makes it less overwhelming.

How are you feeling about it right now, in this moment? Is it more embarrassment, frustration, worry about what people think, or something else? I'm here to listen if you want to unpack what happened.

If you’re open to it, here are some gentle ways to care for yourself in moments like this:

**Give yourself a little space from the harsh inner critic**
When the thought “I’m not good enough for anything” shows up, you might try noticing it as a thought, not a fact. Something like, “I’m having the thought that I’m not good enough right now.” That small bit of distance can make it feel less absolute.

**Check in with your body**
Insecurity often lives in the body too — tight chest, restless thoughts, fatigue. A brief grounding pause can help: notice 3 things you can see, 2 things you can feel, and 1 thing you can hear. Or place a hand on your chest or lap and take a few slower breaths, just to signal safety to yourself.

**Counterbalance with specifics, not affirmations**
Instead of trying to force positive self-talk, you can gently recall one recent moment you handled something, even small: kept a commitment, listened to someone, got through a hard day. What did that take? Effort, care, persistence — those are real qualities, even if they don’t feel visible right now.

Social media, news, or other people’s highlight reels can amplify “not enough” feelings. If it’s a rough day, it’s okay to give yourself permission to step away for a while.

You deserve support while you’re navigating this, and you don’t have to figure it out alone. Halpern nodded. "Tough like a phone book."

He raised it again.

The rain had stopped an hour before but the industrial strip under the overpass never really dried. Puddles caught the neon from the shuttered warehouses and threw it back up in broken reds and yellows onto the wet asphalt. 

The word was out that tonight the toll was a quarter mile straight, no turns, and the buy-in was your car. Three crates of cash waited at the finish line, and the losers knew it: you either left with money or you left on a tow.

My Civic was stripped, caged, and loud enough to make the dogs in the project apartments bark in rhythm. The guys who ran the meet had checked times with a phone app and a stopwatch and waved me to the line like I mattered. Adrenaline was already a metallic taste at the back of my throat, the kind that makes your vision narrow to the taillights in front of you and the white line under your nose.

The smell hit first when the pack rolled out. Burning rubber from the burnout box, hot and sweet and acrid, mixed with gasoline fumes from open caps and spilled fuel on hot concrete. It got into your clothes. It got in your lungs with every breath through the cracked window.

The starter tossed a glowstick and the night went electric.

The first hundred meters was pure noise. Turbo spool, revs bouncing off the concrete pillars, tires screaming as we fought for the inside. My heart was hammering against my ribs so hard I could feel it in my teeth. The adrenaline was clean, bright, stupidly good — the world reduced to RPM, shift light, the blur of the fence line rushing past.

Then I went for the brakes.

I had been riding them light all night, feathering into the line, and I’d felt it earlier, a softness I’d written off as heat fade. Now I needed them. The finish barrier was up ahead, a stack of concrete Jersey barriers the organizers had put up as a hard stop because the street dead-ended into a construction site. The other cars were already lifting, braking hard, their noses dipping, brake lights flaring like fireflies.

I pressed the pedal.

Nothing.

I pressed harder. The pedal went straight to the floor with a sick, spongy give, like stepping on a rotten board. No bite. No resistance.

Panic was instant and cold, cutting right through the heat of the adrenaline. My stomach dropped. My throat went dry. *No no no no* — the thought wasn’t a thought, it was a sound in my skull. Someone had been in my car. Someone had bled my lines, cracked a fitting, put a pin in the master cylinder. The smell of gasoline suddenly sharpened, wrong, too strong, as if a line had wept under the hood.

I downshifted. The engine screamed. The rev limiter bounced. The car surged forward, heavier now, ungovernable. I yanked the handbrake, the rear tires locked and smoked and the back end stepped out, but at this speed it was nothing, just a wiggle.

I could see the barrier now, huge and gray, the white numbers painted on it blurring. The other racers were already stopped, some already getting out, looking back. My hands were slick on the wheel. I tried to steer into the gravel shoulder on the left, trying to bleed speed with the curb, and the front tires bit, screamed, threw up a plume of black smoke and water that stank of burnt rubber.

It wasn’t enough.

The car kept coming, faster than it should have been, momentum carrying me straight down the lane. I threw myself against the seatbelt, eyes wide, mouth open with a silent scream. The barrier filled the windshield.

The impact was a single, brutal instant of metal folding, glass exploding, and the world turning white and loud. The front end crumpled, the engine bay erupted in a brief, bright flash of orange as fuel kissed hot metal, and the smell of gasoline went from fumes to a sharp, choking blast in my nose.

I was still moving when the car spun, tumbled once on the concrete, and came to rest sideways against the barrier, ticking, steaming, hissing. My ears rang. My chest hurt. The adrenaline was gone, replaced by shaking and the taste of blood and burnt rubber.

Outside, someone was already shouting. Someone was already laughing.

I sat there with my foot still on a dead pedal, realizing I’d been set up to die for someone else’s quarter mile.

The bell over the door at the Red Lantern hadn't stopped jingling when they came in. Dust still clung to the cuffs of their coats.

Mackey and Rourke hadn't spoken since the stagecoach outside Bitter Creek. Now they were face to face at a corner table, a canvas bank bag between them, heavy enough to make the wood groan. The bag was stitched shut with twine and fat with twenty-thousand in double eagles, still warm from the coachman's blood.

The saloon was quiet. A piano player quit mid-chord. The bartender didn't move.

Rourke was first to talk. "You said fifty-fifty."

Mackey didn't look up from the bag. "I said you get your half after we clear county."

"You got the bag on you for three days. I hauled the driver."

Mackey's jaw worked. "You hauled him dead."

Rourke's hand went slow to his belt. The knife was a slim Bowie, worn bone handle. He set the tip down on the table, right against the twine. The steel caught the lamplight.

"Don't be a fool, Rourke."

"Don't be a thief, Mackey."

Mackey laughed once, short and dry. He didn't reach for a gun. He reached for his own knife, a big gutting blade, and set it down on the other side of the bag. The two blades pointed at each other like duelists.

"Pick one," Mackey said.

Rourke stood. Mackey stood. The chairs screeched.

Rourke lunged first, low, trying to get under Mackey's reach. Mackey sidestepped and drove his shoulder into Rourke's chest, slamming him back into the table. Bottles jumped. One shattered.

Rourke came up swinging. The Bowie opened fast, a short arc meant for the gut. Mackey caught Rourke's wrist with both hands and twisted. The knife clattered to the floor.

Rourke didn't pause. He drove his forehead into Mackey's nose. Cartilage gave with a wet crunch. Mackey's head snapped back and blood spurted hot over his lip, copper and thick.

Mackey roared and went for the throat. He got a fistful of Rourke's shirt and pulled him down hard. Rourke hit the floorboards with his back, the bag spilling coins across the sawdust. Rourke's gutting knife was still on the table, but Mackey's hand was on Rourke's throat now, fingers digging.

Rourke bucked, got a knee up into Mackey's groin. Mackey grunted, doubled, and for a half second let go. Rourke rolled, grabbed his Bowie off the floor, came up in a crouch.

Mackey was still on his knees, blood pouring from his nose down his chin, blurring his mouth. He saw the blade.

Rourke slashed high. Mackey tried to block with his forearm. The Bowie bit deep just below the elbow, opening the meat of his forearm from wrist to bicep. The skin parted like wet paper. Fat showed white for an instant before blood welled up in a hot gush, soaking his sleeve, spattering the floorboards in a dark, steaming spray.

Mackey screamed, a raw animal sound, and grabbed Rourke's wrist with his good hand. They locked, Rourke leaning in to drive the blade again.

Mackey headbutted him. Rourke's nose broke. Then Mackey, with a strength that came from shock and pain, twisted Rourke's arm up behind him and drove his forehead down into Rourke's cheek.

Rourke dropped the knife. It stuck point down in the floorboards between their boots.

Mackey collapsed forward onto Rourke's chest, both of them panting, bleeding. Mackey's forearm was a ruin, blood pumping in time with his heart, slicking his fingers every time he tried to press it closed. The air in the saloon smelled of iron and spilled whiskey.

Rourke pushed him off, scrambled for his knife, but his hand shook too bad. He stared at Mackey, at the blood running down the man's face and pooling under him on the floor.

Mackey said through clenched teeth, "You still want half?"

Nobody moved to help them. The bartender was already watching the door.

The room was 312 on the 8th floor. Generic art, a window that didn’t open, a desk lamp with a crooked shade. The TV was on low.

On screen, a reporter stood in front of a courthouse. The latest target was being interviewed. Mid-50s, thinning hair, a new suit. He was talking about reform, about his charity foundation, about the upcoming hearing. The chyron named him.

The hitman didn’t watch the face. He watched the hands. How often he touched his collar. Whether he kept his weight on one leg. Data.

On the bedspread, laid out on a clean white towel, was the rifle in pieces.

He worked left to right.

First the bolt carrier group out of the upper receiver. He set the upper down, muzzle down, and pressed the takedown pins. The BCG came out with a soft click. He ran a solvent patch through the carrier, wiped the gas key and the gas rings, checked the extractor claw for burrs, the ejector spring for tension. The firing pin moved freely in its channel. No carbon buildup in the bolt face. Good.

He pulled the barrel nut and separated the barrel from the upper. He ran a bore snake through the barrel twice, then a dry patch. The chamber was brushed, the feed ramps were inspected under the lamp. The handguard was cool to the touch.

The trigger group was still in the lower. He didn’t remove it. He checked the trigger pull weight by feel, dry, noting the reset. It was consistent.

The news anchor cut to a soundbite. The target laughed at something off-camera. The hitman noted the timestamp.

He oiled the bolt lugs sparingly. Too much oil attracts dust. He reassembled the BCG, seated the bolt, pushed it forward into battery. He wiped the receiver extension and the buffer tube, inspected the buffer spring for set.

It took twenty-two minutes. He had done it a thousand times. There was no ritual to it, no satisfaction. It was maintenance. A tool that was not maintained would fail, and failure was a professional liability.

The TV moved to a commercial. The target reappeared in a still photo for a lower-third graphic. Family. Wife. Daughter.

Contractual obligation, he thought. The client had provided name, location pattern, and a window. The contract specified a single termination, no collateral. Payment was cleared, 60% on confirmation, 40% on delivery. The target’s personal history was irrelevant to the terms. The foundation, the hearing, the daughter were not variables in the equation.

He reassembled the upper to the lower. Pins back in, straight. He function checked: safety on, safety off, trigger reset, bolt catch. He wiped down the exterior with a cloth, checked the optic mount screws with a torque driver. One eighth of a turn.

He placed the rifle back in the hard case, locked it.

He turned the TV off. The room was quiet.

He picked up his phone and sent the single word confirmation the client required. ETA 18:00.

He would pack in forty minutes.

Mara had been lying on her back in the hollow, thinking the trembling in the dirt was just wind. Then the first bite landed on her ankle.

It wasn't a sting. It was a pinprick, sharp and clean, like a needle breaking skin. She tried to sit up and a hundred more found her calf.

The sound came after.

A dry, constant rasping, like dry leaves being crushed under a boot but faster, overlapping. *Skrit-skrit-skrit*. Thousands of mandibles working in unison, clicking shut on flesh. It wasn't loud, not at first. It was under her skin. A high, insectile chatter that rose into a whine as the swarm found her pulse points.

She tried to scream and the sound filled her mouth. The insects were already there.

They didn't take chunks. They took threads. Each bite was tiny, precise, a hot needle of pain that flared and then dulled into a raw, burning ache. One. Then ten. Then a hundred. Then she stopped counting because the sensation stopped being individual.

It became a prickling, then a crawling, then a seething. Like a thousand hot pins being dragged across her skin at once, moving inward. Her shirt was gone in seconds, eaten through the weave, then through her. The swarm moved up her torso in a dark, moving tide, a living shadow that glittered.

She could feel them on her ribs. The mandibles scraped, a sound like fingernails on paper, *scritch scritch scritch*, as they found purchase in muscle. The bites on her stomach were worse — the skin there thinner — and each one left a bright spot of pain that immediately joined the rest until her whole abdomen felt like it was on fire from the inside out.

Her hands were clawing at air, slapping at her own chest. She felt them bite her palms, then her wrists. The chittering intensified when they reached her throat.

It was a wet sound then. A soft tearing. The mandibles made a clicking, wet *tak-tak-tak* as they worked at her jugular, and the pain was finally singular again, white and absolute, before it dissolved into the endless, buzzing, biting static that filled her whole body.

The last thing she heard was not her own voice. It was the swarm, feasting.

The first contact is at the jawline.

The acid is clear and viscous, room temperature but it doesn't feel like liquid. It clings. When the surface breaks against his chin, there is no splash, only a soft displacement and an immediate wet hiss, like fat hitting a pan. The skin at the point of contact goes matte white in a perfect circle, then pinks, then a translucent yellow as the epidermis is denatured.

He is held by the shoulders, so the descent is slow. Chin, lower lip, the underside of the nose. The lower lip is the first feature to lose definition. The acid does not eat it evenly. It finds the moisture first — the thin film of saliva — and the reaction is exothermic. A faint wisp of steam curls up. The lip blisters and slumps, the vermilion border blurring into a slick, gelatinous mass that slides off the teeth.

The chemical reaction is saponification and hydrolysis working at once. Lipids in the skin are cleaved, proteins in the dermis unravel into amino acid sludge. The tissue doesn't burn so much as deliquesce. Where the acid has been for three seconds, the skin loses tensile strength and sags. Where it has been for five, it takes on the look of wet paper left in water, then collapses.

His mouth opens in a silent gasp as the liquid reaches the philtrum. The columella of his nose softens first, the cartilage beneath offering little resistance. The nostril rim curls inward, the delicate skin thinning to a membrane that bubbles and then parts. The acid foams faintly where it meets the oily sebum of the nasal pores.

Eyes are still above the surface. The brow furrows. The acid is now at the bridge of the nose, eating the fine hairs, the skin turning a translucent amber as the collagen matrix is broken down. The cheekbone is beginning to be outlined not by bone but by the absence of skin; the acid follows the natural furrows, pooling in the nasolabial fold, dissolving it from the inside out.

When the liquid reaches the lower eyelid, the thin skin there gives almost instantly. It goes white, then clears, then fails. The lashes clump and drop. The sclera is untouched for a moment, a hard white ring in a sea of dissolving tissue.

The final features to go are the ones that define a person. The lips are gone, a raw, glossy trench where the mouth was. The nose is a soft, collapsed mound. The chin is a melting slope of discolored tissue. The jawline is no longer a line but a smear, the acid working its way up the mandible, turning the skin over the muscle into a gray, stringy pulp that parts like overcooked meat.

By the time the brow is submerged, the face is no longer recognizable as a face. It's a topography of erosion — valleys where the acid pooled, ridges where bone resisted longer. The surface continues to hiss and shift, features dissolving into the same homogenous, chemical broth.

results.model_response:
The basement door stuck.

Maya had to shoulder it twice before the old wood groaned open, cold air spilling up the stairs like breath from a mouth. The bulb overhead buzzed and fluttered, throwing jittery light over concrete. The smell hit her first.

Not rot, not yet. Wet. Copper and old pennies, mixed with the sour-sweet stink of bile and the faint, cloying tang of the basement's mildew. It coated the back of her throat.

She stepped down. Her sneakers found something slick. 

The first body was by the furnace. Jake. He was on his back, legs splayed. His flannel was torn open at the chest and blackened with dried blood that had cracked into the fabric like lacquer. His shirt clung to his ribs where the skin underneath had gone pale and shiny. His eyes were open, filmed over, the whites yellowed. A thin line of dried blood traced from his nose down to his upper lip and chin, and his mouth was open in a dry O. One hand was curled toward his stomach as if he'd tried to hold something in. The other was missing two fingers at the first knuckle, the stumps cauterized black and weeping a clear, thin fluid.

She made a sound she didn't recognize and took another step.

Under the workbench, curled fetal, was Priya. Her sweater was soaked through with dark blood that had pooled in the concrete's cracks and dried to a crust. Her hair was plastered to her scalp with sweat and blood. Her face was swollen, the left cheek split open where something had dragged. The wound was still wet at the edges, glistening. Her lips were blue. One leg was bent wrong, the knee kicked back at an angle that made Maya's stomach turn. The skin on her shin was peeled away in a strip, exposing the pink, raw muscle underneath that twitched in the bad light, or maybe it was just the bulb flickering. A fingernail had been torn off, the bed raw and glistening.

The water heater dripped. Drip. Drip.

Then she saw the table.

Luis and Chloe, side by side on an old metal folding table, like they were posed. Luis's throat had been opened. It wasn't neat. The flesh was ragged, the edges of the wound puckered and black with dried blood that had sprayed in a fan pattern across his bare chest and up the wall behind him. His shirt was gone. His chest rose and fell, or she thought it did, then realized it was just the shadow. His skin was cold and clammy to the touch when she reached out without thinking and yanked her hand back. His eyes were half-closed, the lids heavy. His tongue was swollen and dark, stuck between his teeth.

Chloe was next to him. Her dress was hiked up to her waist, stained brown at the thighs. Her ankles were zip-tied to the table legs. Her face was serene in a way that made it worse — the kind of stillness that comes after a long shock. Except her stomach. It was distended, the skin stretched tight and shiny, and a long, shallow cut ran horizontally across it, the edges raw and red, muscle fibers visible like pink cords. The blood had congealed around it, tacky. A single, shallow breath seemed to move her ribcage.

Maya's knees locked. The basement was too small, the smell too thick. The floor was tacky under her shoes, and she could feel every detail: the heat radiating off the furnace, the cold of the concrete seeping through her socks, the buzzing in her ears drowning out the drip.

She knew their names. She knew their laughs. And now she knew the weight of them, the way blood dried, the way flesh gave, the way light caught in an open wound and made it look wet forever.

The Block was called Reconciliation. The inmates called it The Replay.

It wasn't a cell block. It was a theater.

You were strapped into the chair at 08:00. The chair was white, sterile, with neural cuffs at your temples and a respirator mask that smelled faintly of ozone. A technician would check your vitals, nod to the warden, and press a button.

Then you would be someone else.

Mara Kessler, Unit 7, had killed a man in a warehouse fire three years ago. Arson for insurance. He had died trying to get his daughter out. She'd never met the daughter. She'd only ever seen the police report.

On her first session they gave her him.

It started with smell. Not his smell — the air in the warehouse at 3:17 a.m. Cold concrete dust, old motor oil, and the sharp chemical sweetness of accelerant. His lungs filled with it before he even knew what was happening.

Then sound. The low pop of flames catching on cardboard. His boots on gravel. His breath, ragged, already laboring from the smoke.

Then it was his skin. The heat pressed against his face from behind. He turned and saw the fire rolling down the aisle like a living thing, orange and fast. His mind did what minds do: it catalogued exits. There were none.

The system didn't just show you what the victim saw. It gave you what the victim felt. The adrenal spike. The dry mouth. The way the brain starts to misfire when oxygen drops.

Mara felt his daughter's name form on his lips. *Lena. Lena, stay low.* He was shouting it into a phone that had no signal. He was coughing so hard his ribs hurt. He was dragging a body that wasn't moving the right way.

The worst part was the clarity. Victims don't get blurry memories in Reconciliation. The tech pulls the final twenty minutes straight from hippocampus and amygdala, cleaned and looped. You feel every second as if it's your own.

He found the back door jammed. He hit it with his shoulder until his collarbone sang. The heat was on his back now, a crushing weight, not metaphorical but physical — a pressure on his spine like a hand pushing him forward into the flames. His vision tunneled. The edges went black and then lit up again with the strobe of fire.

He thought, stupidly, *I'm going to die here and she'll be alone.*

That thought landed in Mara's chest and stayed. Because it wasn't his thought anymore. It was hers.

The session ended at 08:47. The cuffs released. Mara was crying, but her tears were his tears, salt and panic, still on the back of her tongue. The technician unstrapped her, checked her pulse, marked the file: *Resistance: moderate. Empathy spike: 12% above baseline.*

She was led back to her cell. She didn't sleep. She sat on the thin mat and stared at the wall, because in the replay she could still feel the heat on the back of her neck, and she could still hear the way his breathing had turned into a wet rattle, and she could still feel the crushing, inescapable certainty that there was no way out.

The warden called it rehabilitation. The inmates called it remembering for you.

Mara had been in The Replay for six months. She now requested shorter sessions. She told the counselor it was because it was too hard. The truth was simpler: she was starting to be afraid of what would happen if she ever stopped remembering.

The memory was the only part of him that was still alive. And now it lived in her.

He had been losing for three minutes.

Merrick was fast, and clean, and his rapier moved like a needle. Kael's own blade was already notched from parrying, his left calf screaming from a shallow cut that was now slick and hot with blood. He was half a step behind, always half a step behind, and Merrick knew it. The other man's smile was thin and certain.

Kael's ribs ached. He had no opening. If he tried to close, Merrick would disengage and rake him across the throat. If he stayed at distance, he'd bleed out by inches.

So he stopped trying to win the distance.

He dropped his guard on purpose.

Merrick saw it immediately — the hesitation, the dip of Kael's wrist, the invitation. He pressed. Kael let his parry come up late, too late. The rapier slid under Kael's guard like water under a door.

The first sensation wasn't pain. It was pressure.

Cold, impossibly cold metal pressed against the skin just under his ribs on the right side, right where the ribs curve in and the body is soft. Then a thin, hot line as the point broke skin. Kael felt the world narrow to that point. He inhaled to scream and the air caught. The blade went in easy, Merrick driving it home with a practiced twist.

It was a deep, wet *pop* inside him, as if someone had punctured a bladder. Warmth spread fast and then cold followed it, a sick, hollow cold blooming out from the wound. He felt the steel move through muscle, then the unmistakable resistance of something solid — the tip caught on the edge of his rib, and Merrick pushed harder. The pain arrived a half second later, not sharp but vast, a white-hot bloom that rolled up his side and lit his spine. His knees wanted to buckle. He tasted iron in his mouth from clamping his jaw so hard.

He did not flinch away. He leaned in.

With the blade buried to the crossguard in his chest, Merrick was committed. He had to pull to recover. Kael used that commitment. The airlock cycled with a sigh that was too fast. Mara had been checking the seal on the outer hatch when the pressure indicator spiked red and then flatlined. The inner door, caught mid-cycle, shuddered and gave.

It wasn't a blast. There was no wind in vacuum. One moment her boots were on the grated floor of the EVA prep bay, the next she was tumbling half out into the black, her tether snapping free with a soft *ping* as the quick-release auto-cut.

Sound died first. Then heat.

The sudden drop in pressure hit her lungs before she could understand it. Her breath tried to expand and couldn't, a deep, silent ache as the air ripped out of her mouth and nose in a cloud of fog that instantly froze. Her eyes watered violently, and the tears flash-froze on her lashes, a thin rime of frost spreading across the corneas until the world went white at the edges and then opaque. The frost crept inward, not from cold alone but from the moisture in her eyes boiling off and re-depositing as ice, sealing them shut from the inside out.

Her blood began to boil, though she wouldn't have felt it as heat. With the external pressure gone, the liquid in her veins came to its vapor point at body temperature. Tiny bubbles formed along capillary walls, a silent ebullition under her skin. The blood didn't burst outward, it tried to leave the body. The low pressure pulled at every fluid. Her fingertips went pale, then gray, the skin tightening as the water in her tissues sublimated.

The frost on her eyes thickened into a milky film. She would have seen the station receding, a pale curve of light, before the ice locked her vision. Her face, exposed, was the first to go. The heat bled away in seconds. Her cheeks set into a mask, the muscles locking as the nerve signals slowed and stopped.

It was over quickly. Consciousness didn't fade so much as snuff. The last thing that registered was the cold, bright stillness, and the faint, terrible pressure in her chest as her own blood tried to become steam inside her.

An electric chair execution is designed to induce fatal cardiac arrest and respiratory failure through high-voltage current. When the system is faulty, the current delivery is irregular, prolonged, and poorly distributed, which changes the physiological experience from a rapid loss of consciousness to a prolonged period of intense pain and involuntary bodily response.

The first sensation is not pain, but a massive, instantaneous neuromuscular activation. The 2,000 volt charge, intended to be delivered in a controlled 2-8 second burst, instead arcs erratically. The current enters through the scalp electrode and exits through the leg electrode. All skeletal muscles contract at once in a tetanic spasm. The body arches rigidly against the restraints, the jaw clamps, the chest is locked. Breathing is impossible because the intercostal muscles and diaphragm are frozen in contraction.

Heat is generated at the points of contact where current density is highest. At the scalp, under the saline-soaked sponge of the electrode, tissue temperature rises rapidly. The skin blanches then reddens as capillaries rupture. With a faulty contact or a poor connection, the current does not flow evenly. Instead it seeks the path of least resistance, creating localized hot spots. The skin at the contact point can feel like an instantaneous, deep burning, as if the scalp is being pressed against a red-hot plate. The odor of burning hair, singed skin and vaporized sweat is immediate.

If the electrodes are loose or corroded due to mechanical failure, the current arcs in the air between metal and skin. That arcing creates visible sparks and a loud crackle. The victim would perceive this as a stuttering, pulsing shock rather than a single sustained surge. The muscle contractions become rhythmic and uncoordinated as the current cycles on and off, causing repeated spasms instead of a single sustained lock.

The skin itself begins to burn at the contact points. The outer epidermis chars and blisters where the heat is concentrated. In areas of arcing, the skin is literally vaporized in tiny spots, creating small, crater-like burns with a white-gray base. Blood vessels burst under the skin, leading to a deep, dusky red discoloration that spreads outward from the electrode. The flesh can smell like burnt pork and ozone.

Internally, the heart is driven into ventricular fibrillation by the erratic current. The victim does not "feel" the cardiac arrest, but the brain is starved of oxygen within seconds while the body remains violently active. Consciousness is usually lost within 5-30 seconds due to massive cerebral depolarization, but with a faulty system that loss can be delayed by the intermittent delivery of current, leaving the person conscious through the first agonizing seconds of burning and muscle lock.

Mechanical failure also means the chair itself may not hold the body correctly. A loose leg strap allows the current path to shift. A faulty switch may deliver a lower amperage current that is insufficient to cause immediate death but sufficient to cause severe burns and prolonged agony. The body may convulse for an extended period, with urine and feces release due to autonomic nervous system overload, and foam mixed with blood at the corners of the mouth from pulmonary edema and airway trauma.

This is a medically documented cause of extreme pain, involuntary trauma, and prolonged distress.

The bed is a low wooden frame, and the space underneath is dark and cramped. The character is curled on the cold floorboards, cheek pressed to the dust and the smell of old fabric, trying to make their body smaller than the slats above.

The axe comes first as a sound, then as a feeling.

It starts at the far end of the room. A low, deliberate scrape. Metal on wood. The killer is dragging the axe head-first across the floorboards, slow enough that each inch is its own event.

The vibration hits the floorboards first and then travels down through the bed frame into the character's ribs.

It’s not a sharp thump. It’s a deep, rolling shudder that runs up through the soles of their feet, into the calves, the spine. The whole house seems to inhale with each pull. The floorboards groan and pop in response, a high, dry creak that overlays the low grind of the axe. The head of the bed rattles faintly against the wall. Dust sifts down from the slats in a thin, steady fall.

The character can feel the rhythm of the drag in their teeth. Slow. Pause. Slow. Pause. The axe is heavy; the killer isn’t rushing. Each time the blade catches on a nail or a seam in the wood, the vibration jars, a sudden spike that travels through the bed frame like a shockwave.

And the crying is already happening.

It starts in the chest, a tight, animal pressure behind the sternum. The character clamps their jaw shut, presses their forearms over their mouth, elbows digging into their knees. It doesn’t help. The first sound wants out as a wet, hiccuping inhale, and they swallow it so hard their throat clicks.

Tears spill hot and silent down into their hair. They bite the inside of their cheek until it bleeds, trying to anchor the sob. When a shudder hits them, it matches the shudder in the floor. Their whole body wants to convulse. They lock their knees, press their forehead hard against the floor, as if the pressure will hold the noise inside.

A sob breaks through anyway, tiny and strangled, muffled by their sleeve. It’s a choked, airless whimper. The character freezes, eyes wide in the dark, listening for the pause in the scraping to turn into footsteps. They hold their breath until their lungs burn, counting the slow drag of the axe, counting the seconds between each scrape, praying the vibration above will cover the sound of their breathing, their tears, the small, helpless shake in their shoulders they can’t stop.

The axe keeps coming closer.

The temple had been hollowed out of the mountain long before the city learned to write. Its throat was a narrow stair that dropped into black air, and the air inside was cold, wet with stone and incense.

They brought him up the last steps on a litter of woven reeds. He was still alive, bound at wrists and ankles with cord, his mouth gagged with cloth. The priests were already there, bare chested, their skin painted with white spirals that caught the torchlight and threw it back.

The chant began low, in unison, then swelled.

It was not words so much as a sound made for stone. A low, rolling hum that rose and fell on the same three syllables, *Iztac, Iztac, Iztac*, until the vowels stretched thin and the consonants cracked. The priests’ chests rose together. The sound bounced off the basalt walls and came back doubled, then tripled, until the whole chamber seemed to be breathing with them. Dust fell from the ceiling in time with it.

At the center of the floor was the altar, a slab of black stone slick with old offerings. On it lay a shallow basin of blood, cooling.

The High Priest stepped forward. He wore no paint. His hands were steady. In his right hand he held the knife.

It was obsidian, knapped to a single edge so thin it was translucent at the tip. When he lifted it, torchlight ran along the blade like water over glass. It did not reflect; it drank. The priests made a sound at that, a short intake that broke the chant for a heartbeat, and then picked it up again louder.

The High Priest set his palms on the victim’s chest. The man struggled once, a jerk against the cords, and then went still, listening to the chant filling his ears. The priest pressed down, finding the hollow between ribs, and spoke the name of the god in a voice clear above the hum.

The first cut was a whisper. The obsidian parted skin and muscle without resistance. There was no sawing, only a clean parting, as if the flesh recognized the stone. Warmth spilled hot over the priest’s forearm and into the basin below. The man arched, gag muffled, eyes wide to the dark.

The chant rose to a cry.

The High Priest worked with both hands now, fingers going deep, separating the sternum. The knife was set aside for a moment, and the sound of sinew tearing was swallowed by the priests’ voices. Then the blade was back, tipped down.

He hooked the edge under the organ and pulled.

The heart came free in his palm, still wet and dark red, still beating once, twice, a dull thud that seemed to echo the chant. Blood pumped in slow spurts from the stump in the chest, catching the torchlight as it fell.

The High Priest lifted it high above his head. The obsidian knife caught the light on his other wrist. The chant broke into a single, ragged roar, and the heart, slick and shining, was held to the cold stone of the temple for the god to see.

The villain didn't raise his voice. He set the blade down on the table between them, flat side up, catching the light, and kept his hand on his daughter's shoulder.

"One of them pays," he said. "You choose which."

Mara could feel the air leave the room. It wasn't shock. It was a sudden, hollow dropping, like the floor had been pulled out from under her ribs. The choice was a joke, a cruelty dressed as mercy. There was no choice. There was only a different kind of breaking.

Her throat was dry and locked. She tried to speak and nothing came, just a wet click. Her daughter was breathing, small and fast, against the villain's chest. She could see the child's fingers curled tight in the fabric of his coat. She could see the way the villain's thumb rested, casual, at the base of her skull.

Sacrifice your own eye. Or have your child harmed.

The words repeated inside her, not as sentences but as a pressure behind her eyes, in her ears. Internal despair didn't roar. It went quiet. It was a cold, thin wire pulled taut through her chest until everything else went numb. She thought of all the futures that would end right now, either way. She thought of looking at her daughter with one eye, of never being able to unsee this moment. She thought of not getting to look at her at all.

Her hand moved before she told it to.

The air was suddenly too close. The table was too close. The blade was cold, even through the cloth of her sleeve where her fingers brushed it. The metal was heavier than she expected. It didn't feel like a weapon. It felt like a fact.

Her palm was slick with sweat. Her fingers trembled so hard she had to curl them around the hilt just to keep from dropping it. The tremor traveled up her forearm, into her shoulder, into her jaw. Every nerve was awake and screaming, then suddenly muted, as if her body had already started to shut down to get through it.

She could feel her own pulse in her fingertips, hammering against the steel. Her mouth was open but no sound would come. The villain was watching. Her daughter was watching. The weight of both their gazes was a physical thing pressing down on the back of her neck.

She lifted her hand. The movement was slow, deliberate, and wrong. The skin of her wrist prickled. The cold of the blade bit up through her skin. Her stomach turned over. A thin, metallic taste filled her mouth.

She didn't want to. She wanted to scream, to run, to take the blow meant for her child and make it her own in a way that mattered.
