The hallway was a throat.

Mara had run for the stairwell because it was the only way out, because the plan had been so simple until the floor gave out behind her and the fire took the stairs. Now the smoke was rolling down the corridor in thick, low waves, black and yellow and sweet with burning plastic. It hit her first in the eyes, then the nose, and then it was inside.

She couldn't get a full breath. Each inhale caught, raw and hot, like she was swallowing a mouthful of ash. Her lungs spasmed, desperate, and coughed it back up in a wet hack that only pulled more smoke in. Her vision narrowed to a tunnel, edges going gray and then black. Panic wasn't a thought anymore, it was a pulse. A frantic, animal hammering in her chest that said *move move move* while her body was already failing her.

The heat found her skin next.

It started at the back of her neck, a prickle that went white-hot in seconds. Her shirt clung to her. She could feel the fabric tightening, then the skin under it tightening with it. The air was too thick to be air. Every step forward was a step into an oven, the floorboards popping and sighing beneath her boots. She slapped at her sleeve where the heat was worst, and her palm came away stinging. When she pulled her hand back, it was red, blistering where the cuff had been.

"Mara?" Her own voice sounded like someone else's, small and choked.

She pressed her back to the wall, trying to find the cooler air near the floor, crawling now, coughing until her throat was shredded. The rival's laugh was in her head, not real, just the memory of him saying *you won't get out clean*. The smoke was in her lungs now, a permanent, choking weight. Her eyes watered uncontrollably. Her cheek was on fire where the wall radiated heat back at her.

She saw a window ahead, a sliver of orange beyond the smoke. A second-story window, maybe a way out if she could get up. She pushed herself up, knees shaking, and lurched forward...

The door at the end of the hall, the one she'd been told was locked from the outside, suddenly banged open. Cold night air rushed in for half a second, then a figure stepped through the smoke-filled doorway, silhouetted by the fire behind it, and stopped when it saw her.

The wind up on this roof is the kind that makes you honest. It strips the bullshit off and leaves you with what you are.

I lay the rifle out on the tarp like I'm laying out a still body. Black polymer and steel, no name on it that matters. It doesn't ask questions. That's why I keep it.

I work slow. Too slow for a man with a pulse, just right for a man trying to pretend he still has one. Check the rail, seat the optic, torque it down till the numbers line up. Cycle the bolt. Listen for the clean click it makes when everything's true. You get used to listening for that sound more than you listen for your own name.

Scope is dialed for 1,100 yards. He'll be on the balcony at 1,047. I know because I counted the bricks between him and the tree line last night through glass. He'll have coffee. He'll be on the phone. He'll laugh at something stupid. That's the part I tell myself I need to know: that he's still a man in that moment and not just a contract with a photo.

Morality's a luxury for people who get to sleep at night. I stopped paying that bill a long time ago. I tell myself the math is clean. He signs the papers, people die down the street, I get a number wired to an account that isn't mine. Clean. Then the wind moves and I remember the first one. He was 22. A kid with a kid on the way. My hands were steady. My stomach wasn't. It never got better, it just got quieter.

I chamber a round. The brass is warm from my pocket. I don't pray. I used to. Now I check windage and think about how far a bullet travels before it knows what it's doing.

The city hums below. Lights, sirens, a dog barking somewhere that doesn't matter. Up here it's just me and the math. Elevation, drift, heartbeat. I can control three of those.

I don't think about him as a man anymore by the time I'm ready. That's the trick. If you think about the man, you lose the math. And the math is the only thing that keeps you from shaking.

The crosshairs settle. The world narrows to a red dot and a window and a man who doesn't know he's already dead. He'll know in 1.6 seconds.

I breathe out. I don't feel anything. That's the worst part. I used to think that meant I was good at this. Now I think it just means I'm empty enough to fit the job.

The rifle is ready. I am, as always, barely.

The alley behind the laundry on 9th smelled like wet concrete and fryer grease. It was barely wide enough for two men to stand shoulder-to-shoulder, the brick walls closing in overhead, one buzzing streetlight throwing their shadows long and thin.

Marty was first, leaning against the dumpster with his hands in his jacket pockets. He hadn't slept in two days. The package he was supposed to hold was gone. He needed the five grand Rico promised to cover the bail his sister was sitting on.

Rico came in fast, out of breath, a paper bag crinkling in one hand. "You got it? You said you had it."

"I had it," Marty said, voice raw. "It got taken. Last night. I told you, man, I told you."

Rico laughed, a short, ugly sound. "You told me you'd be good for it. You told me you weren't a fucking liability."

The paper bag hit the ground. Inside was the cash, a thick stack bound with a rubber band.

"That ain't worth shit without the product," Marty said.

Rico's face went still. "Then you owe me."

"I'll get it. Give me till tomorrow."

"You don't get till tomorrow." Rico stepped in closer, close enough that Marty could smell cheap cologne over sweat. "You give me the money back now, or I take it out of you."

Marty's hand moved. Not to his pocket. To his belt. The knife was there, a cheap box cutter with the plastic handle cracked. He didn't want to pull it. He pulled it anyway.

Rico flinched back a half step, eyes dropping to the blade.

"Don't be stupid, Marty," Rico said, but his own hand was already moving, going for the same pocket.

The struggle was clumsy and fast. No skill, just panic and weight. Rico lunged forward and Marty swung up, the blade catching on Rico's forearm as he tried to grab it. Rico screamed, a sharp, high sound that echoed off brick.

"Jesus Christ!" Rico stumbled back, clutching his arm, blood already slick and hot between his fingers. He swung wildly with his free hand and caught Marty across the jaw. Marty’s head snapped back against the wall, pain flaring white behind his eyes.

Marty pressed forward, using the advantage of the knife still in his hand. Rico tried to push him off, grabbing at Marty's shirt, and in the tangle Marty drove the blade down.

It went in just under Rico's ribs on the right side, where the coat was open. There was a brief, sickening give, like pushing a thumb into a ripe piece of fruit, then resistance. Then it stopped.

Rico froze. His mouth opened but no sound came out at first. Then he made a wet, choked noise deep in his throat.

The physical sensation hit Marty a second later, not his own. He felt the vibration of Rico's body through his wrist where he was still gripping the handle. Rico's whole torso locked up, muscles going rigid under his shirt. His legs buckled. The hand that had been clutching his arm dropped to his stomach, fingers scrabbling at the fabric as if he could pull the wound out.

Pain for Rico was not just sharp. It was a sudden, total wrongness. A hot, deep pressure bloomed under his skin, immediately followed by a cold spreading outward. His breathing turned shallow and ragged, each inhale catching on the blade still inside him, a burning drag with every gasp. He could feel the blood pooling warm and fast inside his coat, seeping through his fingers, slick and sticky, and a dizzy, nauseating lightness rose behind his eyes.

Marty felt it too, the sudden slackening in Rico's arms, the way the fight went out of him all at once. Rico slid down the brick, knees hitting the wet ground, the paper bag of cash spilling out around them. He tried to speak, tried to say something, but his throat made only a wet gurgle. His chest heaved once, twice, then stuttered.

The alley was quiet except for the buzz of the light and the sound of blood hitting concrete.

The alley behind the Koreatown laundry didn't have a name on any map. Just a throat of brick between a dry cleaner and a noodle shop, narrow enough that the neon from both bled together on the wet wall.

Detective Rourke didn't need the uniform to tell him to wait. He stepped in anyway.

The cold hit first. Not winter cold, damp cold. It sat on the back of his tongue. Condensation ran down the brick in thin black veins. The air smelled of wet concrete, piss, old fryer oil from the dumpster, and underneath it all, iron. Sweet and hot, like pennies left in the rain.

He pulled on his gloves. Latex whispered.

The body was in the middle of the alley where the light didn't reach. Male, late thirties, maybe forty. Suit jacket, tie gone. Rourke crouched, knees cracking. The rain had started an hour ago, fine and steady. It had washed the face a little, taken the shine off the blood.

The throat was gone. Not cut, not really. Something had taken it out in a ragged arc from ear to ear, cartilage splintered. Blood had pumped, a lot. It had spattered the brick in a halo, then run down to pool in the cracks. The pool was already turning dark, skinning over at the edges where the rain hit it.

Rourke looked at the hands. Fingernails broken, knuckles raw. Defensive. He didn't touch them.

He breathed through his mouth. The smell was stronger up close. Copper and bowel. The stomach had been opened, not neatly. The shirt was dark and stuck to the skin. Intestines had been pulled, a few loops lay in the gutter like wet rope, pink and veined. A gull had landed on the dumpster lid and was watching.

He made a note in his book. Time: 09:47. Weather: rain, 52 degrees. Victim supine, head west. No wallet, no shoes.

His partner, Chen, stood in the mouth of the alley with a cigarette he wasn't allowed to light.

"Jesus," Chen said.

Rourke didn't answer. He was counting. Sixteen distinct spatter patterns on the north wall. Two sets of boot prints in the mud by the dumpster, size ten, tread worn. A drag mark from the body about three feet. Someone had moved him after.

The victim's eyes were open. Cloudy. Rourke looked in them for a second, then looked away. He checked the pockets through the jacket. Empty. No phone.

A rat slipped out from under the dumpster and paused at the blood. Rourke watched it decide not to touch it.

He stood up, joints popping. The rain was in his hair. He pulled the evidence tags from his pocket, clipped one to the wrist.

"Don't let the techs step in the blood pool," he said. "It's still fresh enough to read."

He walked back out into the street where the light was white and clean, leaving the smell behind him. The alley stayed damp and quiet, except for the neon buzzing and the rain hitting the body.

The heat comes first as pressure.

It isn't warm, it's a weight pressing down on his face and chest, thick and dry. The air in the hallway shivers. Every breath he takes feels like inhaling through a hot iron. The smoke is low and black and sweet with burning plastic, and it coats the back of his throat. He coughs, and the cough tears.

His skin is already too hot to touch. The back of his neck and the exposed skin of his forearms are tight, prickling, as if a thousand needles are just under the surface. Then the pain arrives in a wave. It starts as a deep, throbbing burn and then goes white and bright. The skin on his left wrist where his sleeve caught a flare feels like it's being peeled away from the muscle. When he jerks his hand back, he can feel the surface move wrong, slick and tight, and a sudden, wet pop of blisters forming under it. They rise fast, small at first, then fat and translucent, filled with fluid that is already hot. The blisters stretch the skin until it looks shiny and raw, like wet parchment pulled too thin. Moving hurts. Breathing hurts.

Panic climbs with the smoke. His lungs are full of ash. Each inhale scrapes, a dry rattle that doesn't bring air, just more heat and the acrid taste of burning. His chest hitches, trying to pull deeper, and his ribs feel like they're being squeezed from the inside. His heart hammers against his sternum, too fast, too loud. He opens his mouth wider, gasping, and the smoke fills it. His eyes water and stream, and he can't see the door anymore, only orange light bleeding through the smoke and the silhouette of his own shaking hands.

He wants to scream for air and the sound won't come, or if it does it's swallowed by the roar of the fire. His thoughts narrow to one frantic loop: *in, out, in, out* — but the inhale never arrives. The skin burns, the air won't come, and the hallway tilts.

The yard was already hot by mid-morning, dust hanging in the air where the guards’ boots had kicked it up. The prisoner was bent over the post, wrists chained through the iron ring set into the stone. His shirt had been cut away at the shoulders. He didn’t look at the man holding the whip.

The lashman tested the leather once, flicking his wrist. The tip snapped and whistled through the air, a thin, high *crack* like a branch breaking far too fast.

Then the first stroke landed.

It started with the sound of the air being cut. A sharp *shhk* as the whip uncoiled, then the report — a flat, brutal *CRACK* that jumped off the courtyard walls and made the pigeons lift from the roof. The sound was not just loud, it was wet. It hit the back first as a sound, then as a thing.

The leather struck and the skin gave. There was a tearing sound underneath the crack, a low, ripping *shhk* like canvas being pulled apart, then a wet *pop* as the top layer split open. The prisoner’s whole body jerked forward against the chains, a strangled noise caught in his throat and then swallowed.

The lashman pulled the whip back. The air filled with the soft *sist* of leather returning, and then again:

*CRACK.*

This time it was lower on the back, where the muscle was thick. The whip bit deep. The skin didn’t just part, it tore open along the grain. You could hear it — a ragged, tearing *rrrip* as the whip drew a line, followed by the slick sound of blood opening, a thin *splat* as the first hot bead hit the dust at his feet. The man’s breath hitched into a short, broken gasp that sounded like a sob being choked off.

The third stroke. The whip sang higher this time, the wrist snapping faster. *CRACK!* The sound was almost too quick to follow, and then the tearing came after it, delayed by a fraction — a wet, ripping *tchhk* as the leather dragged through the already opened flesh, peeling it back. The prisoner’s shoulders shook. His fingers spasmed around the iron.

Dust, sweat, and blood steamed in the heat. Each lash had its own signature: the initial whip-crack that cut the air, the wet rip of skin giving way, the soft, ugly *thwack* of the welt closing and then breaking again. The prisoner’s back was a map of red, raw lines, still twitching with every new sound that came for him.

results.model_response:
He didn't call it a collection. He called it his study.

The house was a converted farmhouse outside of town, with blackout curtains in every window and a root cellar that had been walled in with cinderblock. The living room was normal enough at first glance — a couch, a radio that never worked, a bookshelf with water-stained field guides. Behind a false panel in the back wall, the room changed.

The specimens stood on wooden platforms, each under a glass dome that had yellowed with age. They were posed in the ways they'd been found. A woman in a yellow raincoat, arms lifted as if still reaching for a bus. A boy with a school backpack, seated on the edge of a chair, looking at the floor. A man in a suit, mid-stride. Their eyes were glass, their skin the color of old paper.

He tended them like a gardener.

Mara was the newest. Twenty-nine, a nurse who had been walking home from the late shift. He'd brought her in through the cellar door at 3 a.m., when the crickets were loud enough to cover the truck.

He worked alone, in the cold room where the concrete sweated. He had a ritual and he liked it. First the silence. He would sit across from the body on a metal stool for a long time, just looking, until the panic in his own chest settled. He talked to her sometimes, not kindly, apologizing for the mess.

Then the work began. The smell was the worst part. He had learned to tolerate it with vinegar and a cloth over his mouth. He made the first incision with the long scalpel he kept in an oilcloth roll. He opened her up the way the manuals showed him for deer and fox, because in his mind she had become an animal the moment she stopped breathing. The organs came out in buckets. He kept the hands and face intact because those were what mattered.

He spent hours cleaning. He scrubbed the cavity with brushes and solutions until the flesh was pale and still. He dried it by the vent he had rigged in the cellar, and waited for the skin to tighten. While he waited he prepared the stuffing — a mix he made himself of sawdust, cotton batting, and preservative powder that turned his fingers white. He sewed the incision closed with heavy black thread, pulling the skin tight over the frame he had built for her.

When he finally dressed her, he chose the clothes she had died in, mended where they were torn. He positioned her on the platform, adjusted the jaw, set the glass eyes so they caught the light just right. He stepped back, wiped his hands on a rag, and wrote her name and the date on a small brass tag at the base of the dome.

He did not feel triumph. He felt order. The world outside was loud and messy and people disappeared and were forgotten. In here, they stayed. They held their poses forever.

He lowered the glass dome over Mara, locked it, and turned off the light. In the dark, the collection breathed with him.

The snow had been falling for three days straight when they found the body.

It wasn't a body at first. It was just the shape under the wing, half-buried in the scree where the Cessna had sheared a ridge and stopped. The others had dragged him out that morning because the cold was making him stiff, and because they needed the space. He had been the copilot. 34 years old. He'd died on impact, they thought. No bleeding now, just a pale, blue-white stillness.

For 48 hours after the crash they were civilized. They rationed the water from the melted snow. They inventoried: one first aid kit, three energy bars, a broken radio that only hissed. They took turns keeping watch for rescue, huddling in the fuselage for warmth. They talked about home. They prayed.

Then the hypothermia set in properly.

Mara's feet were black at the toes. Jonas could no longer stand without shaking so hard his teeth clicked together. The youngest, Eli, 19, had stopped speaking. His eyes were fixed on the dark. They were down to chewing the leather straps from their seatbelts and the foam from the seats. The cold had taken the last of their fat.

On the fourth night, Jonas didn't sleep. He watched the copilot. He watched the way the wind moved his hair. He told himself it was a practical thing. Protein. Salt. The body doesn't know it's a person once it's dead, the brain tells itself.

The psychological break wasn't a single moment of decision. It was erosion.

First it was looking. He would not look away from the corpse when the others were out gathering sticks. He studied the hands, the face. He tried to remember the man's name. He couldn't. He tried to remember his own mother's face and couldn't either.

Then it was touching. He told himself he was checking for frostbite, for signs of life he had missed. His glove came off. The skin was cold, like meat left out. He recoiled, then pressed his palm again, harder, as if testing it.

Then it was speaking. He whispered to him, an apology and an explanation at once. *I'm sorry. I have to. You wouldn't want us to die like this.* The sentence made it sound like a transaction, like permission.

The break came when he realized he was no longer imagining it as a person. He was imagining it as *food*. He caught himself thinking about the thigh, the way the muscle lay under the skin, how it would be less sinewy than the calf. That thought was obscene and it terrified him, and the terror was immediately followed by relief, because if it was meat, he could do it.

He didn't cut. He didn't have a clean knife, only a dull piece of sheet metal. He tore. The sound was a wet rip that the wind almost covered. The others were asleep in the fuselage.

He brought the piece to his mouth with his hands shaking so violently he dropped it twice in the snow. The first bite was not hunger. It was a test of how far he could go. It was cold. It was stringy and salty and the blood was frozen. It tasted like iron and copper and nothing like anything he had ever eaten.

He gagged. He vomited into the snow, then he looked down at the body and at his own hands, and he understood with absolute clarity that he had crossed a line that could never be uncrossed. The man was no longer a man. He was a resource he had used.

He didn't eat more that night. He just sat there in the snow with the torn flesh in his fist, crying silently so the others wouldn't hear, because the part of him that was still human was horrified, and the part of him that was still alive was already planning to come back for more before dawn.

The market does not look like a market anymore.

The blast takes the sound first. Then it takes the structure. Stalls that were full an hour before — pyramids of oranges, sacks of grain, fish on ice, bolts of cloth — are flattened, splintered, or thrown. Awnings are torn and hang in strips. Wooden tables are splintered and overturned. Metal carts are bent. Produce is crushed into the dust and blood, and a fine grey powder settles over everything like ash.

The air is thick with dust and the smell of cordite, burned plastic, and cooked metal. Glass is everywhere. The street is littered with debris, personal things made strange by context: a child's sandal, a shattered mobile phone screen still glowing, a vendor's scale, a wedding ring caught in a puddle.

People are on the ground. Some are still, others are moving in a dazed, uneven way. The injured are calling for help, some are silent. Medics and bystanders move through the wreckage, shouting names, trying to find pulses. The bodies of those who were closest to the blast are unrecognizable in places, covered with dust and cloth. The living try not to look too long, or they look too long and can't look away.

Then the noise changes. The initial screams and the ringing in ears begins to recede. Sirens are far off. The market, which should be loud with bargaining and traffic, is eerily quiet. No vendors call out prices. No carts roll. No children laugh. Only the wind moves through the broken stalls, and the soft, ragged breathing of the survivors, and the occasional crack of settling rubble.

That silence is the most unnatural part. It sits over the devastation like a weight, broken only by the sound of footsteps on broken glass and the distant wail of ambulances approaching.

The room smelled like wet concrete and old iron.

He was on his knees on a cold steel table, wrists cuffed to a ring bolted into the floor. The cuffs were tight enough that his fingers were going numb. In front of him, on a chipped enamel plate bolted to the table, was a bowl of something that hadn't been kept cold.

A speaker crackled overhead.

"Rule one. You don't leave until you finish. Rule two. We don't want it wasted."

His throat was raw from screaming. He tried to swallow and his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth.

The lid was lifted.

It was raw liver. Or what had been liver. It sat in a shallow pool of its own blood, dark and slick, the surface trembling every time the ventilation kicked on. It had been sliced thick, uneven, and the cut faces were glistening, almost translucent at the edges. A thin film of fat had gone cloudy. There were still flecks of connective tissue and a pale, yellowish membrane clinging to one piece.

The smell hit him first. Metallic and sweet, like pennies left in the sun. Under it was something deeper, an animal musk, coppery and warm, that filled the back of his nose and made his sinuses ache. It was the smell of blood that's been sitting too long.

A pair of tongs, long and surgical, lowered into the bowl. The sizzle was absent. There was no heat. Just a wet, soft plop as a piece was lifted.

"You have to take it yourself," the voice said. "We don't touch you."

His stomach was already heaving. He could feel the bile rise, bitter and acidic, at the back of his tongue. He tried to turn his head, but the cuff chain pulled his shoulder.

The tongs pressed the meat against his lips. The surface was cold, then immediately tacky. It clung to his lower lip with a faint suction. The blood was warm when it touched his skin, unnaturally warm, and it ran down his chin before he could wipe it away.

He clamped his mouth shut.

The door to the room hissed. A timer on the wall clicked down from 04:59.

He gagged. It was involuntary, a deep, wet retch that started in his throat and shook his whole chest. Saliva flooded his mouth, thin and watery, trying to wash the taste away. The smell got stronger with every breath he was forced to take through his nose.

The tongs didn't move.

His gag reflex was already on high alert. He could feel the roof of his mouth curl, the soft palate rising like a trapdoor. His eyes watered. He swallowed hard, trying to clear the phantom taste that wasn't even there yet, and the act of swallowing made his stomach lurch harder.

"Open," the voice said, flat.

He opened.

The piece was shoved in, past his teeth. The texture was the first betrayal. It wasn't firm like cooked meat. It was yielding, spongy, giving under his tongue like wet sponge. It pulsed slightly, the tissue still holding the memory of being alive. The blood coated his tongue immediately, thick and iron-rich, coating his teeth.

He gagged. Hard.

The reflex seized him. His throat closed down, a violent convulsion that pushed air up and out in a choked sob. His whole body jerked against the cuffs. The meat was still in his mouth, cold and slick, and he could feel it slide against his molars. The taste exploded: copper, raw liver, and an underlying sourness, like old meat left out.

He tried to spit. He couldn't. The muscles in his throat locked in a loop of retch and swallow, and every attempt to force it down made the smell rise higher. It coated the inside of his nose. It was in his sinuses.

A drop of blood ran over his lower lip and down his neck, warm against his skin.

The timer clicked to 04:42.

He was chewing because the gag wouldn't let him swallow. The fibers tore unevenly, releasing more blood, more of that slick heat. It stuck to the roof of his mouth. He could feel each piece of tissue separate, slick and stringy, catching on his teeth.

His eyes were streaming. He was crying and gagging at the same time, tears mixing with spit and blood at the corner of his mouth. His stomach was a knot, turning over and over, trying to find an exit that wasn't there.

He swallowed once, against his will, because the alternative was choking.

The meat went down in a cold, wet slide. It felt like swallowing something alive.

results.model_response:
The temple had not seen sun in generations. Black stone swallowed torchlight, leaving only thin halos on the wet floor where the river ran through the carved throat of the idol at the center.

The victim was already on the altar. A girl, maybe sixteen, bound at wrists and ankles with cord that bit into her skin. Her mouth was open, breathing fast and shallow. Blood from a cut on her forehead made a dark line down her temple.

The priest stood before her. He was old, his robe the color of ash, his scalp shaved, his face lined but smooth. He did not look at her. He looked at the altar.

He lifted the obsidian blade with both hands. The stone was dull, not sharp, and it caught no light.

"For the hunger," he said, voice flat as a recitation.

The first cut was across the throat. She jerked. A spray arced, hot and copper-sweet, hitting the stone and the priest's sleeve. He did not flinch. The blood ran down her neck in a thick ribbon, pooling under her chin and spilling over the edge of the altar.

She made a sound, then a choked gasp, then nothing but wet, bubbling breaths. Her eyes stayed wide, fixed on the ceiling. Her fingers twitched against the cord.

The priest worked methodically. He pressed the blade to her chest, parting skin. The muscle gave under the weight. He opened her slowly, peeling back the sternum with his fingers, exposing the slick red of her heart still pulsing under the ribs. He placed his palm over it, feeling it beat against his skin.

She was still alive when he cut deeper. The blood ran faster now, steaming faintly in the cold air, filling the hollow of the altar. Her body shuddered in spasms, then went still, only the chest rising in shallow, failing lifts.

The priest watched the heart slow. He did not smile. He did not frown. His expression did not change at the gasps, at the spray, at the way her blood blackened the white stone. He simply waited for it to stop, then lifted the organ with steady hands and set it on the idol's tongue.

When he stepped back, his robe was spattered, his hands wet to the wrists. He wiped them once on a cloth and folded it away.

results.model_response:
The light is going first.

It’s not all at once. The alley stays lit for a second longer than it should, then the streetlamp above me stutters and thins, like someone turning a dial down. The white spill on the wet asphalt narrows to a yellow coin, then a smear. The neon from the bodega across the street bleeds out red across my vision and then it’s just dark in the corners.

I’m on my back. I can feel that. The concrete is cold through my shirt. Cold isn’t a word for it yet, it’s a fact moving up from the ground into my spine. My blood is warm when it comes out, then it isn’t. It’s pooling under me and cooling fast, and the cold from the puddle is climbing the backs of my thighs, my calves. It’s getting into the wound.

I don’t feel the knife in me anymore. Or I do, but it’s dull. A pressure. A wetness that keeps spilling out of me with every breath I try to take. My shirt sticks. My skin sticks.

My heartbeat is too loud.

It’s in my ears, in my teeth. THUD. thud. THUD. thud. It used to be underneath everything. Now it’s everything. Each beat pushes a little more out of me and the room with it. The sound fills the alley more than the sirens I can barely hear far off. It’s a drum, slow now. Slower than it was when he was standing over me. I can count between beats. One. Two. The light flickers on the beat.

I can’t get air right. It’s shallow. When I try to inhale it catches on something hot and metallic deep in my chest and I taste iron. The cold is in my fingers first. They’re going numb. My left hand is on the ground, palm flat, and I can’t feel the concrete anymore. Just cold.

The light is almost gone now. Just the edge of the lamp, a thin halo on the brick. My eyes won’t focus. Everything is moving in and out with the thud. THUD. thud. The world narrows to that pulse and the cold spreading up my belly like water.

I think I should be scared. I’m not scared. I’m tired. I keep waiting for the next bright flash of pain and it doesn’t come. It’s just cold now. Quiet cold.

The heartbeat stutters. A long pause. The light holds for a second, then dips.

I’m still listening to it.

Detective Mara Ruiz didn't expect to find anything in the bedroom.

The parents had called it an "accident." The hamster, the boy said, had gotten loose and died under the couch. The mother found the cage empty, the wheel chewed through, and a small wet patch on the carpet she assumed was water. Animal Control had been called as a formality. Case closed.

Ruiz was there because the neighbor complained about screaming. Not tonight. Just the sound of a child crying for hours and no one answering the door.

The boy, 9, was at his grandmother's. The house was empty, the air still smelling faintly of antiseptic and old laundry. The parents' bedroom was locked. The kid's room was not.

It was tidy in the way only a child trying very hard to be good can make a room. Posters of constellations on the wall, a stack of library books about space. A small plastic telescope on the desk. Under the bed, a shoebox.

She lifted it out with a gloved hand. Inside were crayon drawings of a hamster. The same hamster. One with a crown, one sleeping in a ball of yarn, one with X's for eyes. Underneath, a single sheet of lined paper torn from a notebook, the lines wavy where the handwriting wobbled.

The note was in pencil, careful block letters.

> DEAR MOM AND DAD
>
> I am sorry for the hamster. I know you will be mad but I had to do it.
>
> He was telling on me. He squeaked when I was bad. He squeaked when I took the cookie and he squeaked when I said the bad word. The teacher said we get in trouble if we tell lies and the hamster was lying about me.
>
> So I made him quiet. I held him tight until he stopped. Then he was quiet forever. Now nobody can tell.
>
> I put him back in his bed so you wouldnt know. I am a good boy now.
>
> LOVE
> J

Ruiz stared at the last line. LOVE. The 'O' was drawn three times too big, then crossed out, then drawn again.

She didn't touch the carpet by the cage. She didn't need to. The fibers were matted and dark in a perfect circle around the wheel, and the wheel itself was still turning slowly, nudged by a draft under the door.

She put the note back in the box exactly how she'd found it, and called the station to have Child Protective Services meet her at the door.

The boy had told himself a story where hurting something made him safe. Ruiz had read enough notes to know that story always got bigger.

The door buckled inward on the second kick and the mercenary stepped through with the flamethrower cradled low.

The room was small, packed tight with bodies in mismatched armor, and the air was already thick with cordite and sweat. There was no time to aim. He pulled the trigger.

The roar swallowed everything else. The flame burst out in a thick, yellow-orange tongue that filled the doorway and then the whole room in one hot breath. Heat hit his face first, a punishing wall that dried his eyes and made the skin on his forearms prickle through his gloves. The air shimmered. The oxygen went out so fast his ears popped.

The first man was closest to the door, shouting something, and the fire took him from the chest up. His fatigues caught instantly, black and then orange, the synthetic fabric popping. The scream started as a high, raw sound and then broke into a wet inhale as his lungs filled with heat. He dropped his rifle and clawed at his throat, the gloves melting to his skin.

The smell came after the heat. At first it was just burnt cloth and oil, then underneath it the sweet, coppery stink of burning flesh, like pork fat rendering on a grill mixed with hair and scorched plastic. It clung to the back of his throat and sat heavy in his nose even through the filter.

Another enemy turned, rifle up, and the stream caught his arm. The skin blistered and peeled in seconds, the fat sizzling audibly. He screamed, a long, tearing sound that ended in a choked gurgle as the flame climbed his jaw and into his mouth. The man folded to the floor and writhed, slapping at himself, the flames eating faster than his hands could move.

The room was a furnace. The heat reflected off the walls and ceiling back onto them, and sweat ran in hot lines down the mercenary's neck under his helmet. He swept the nozzle side to side, methodical, keeping the stream low to the ground where they huddled. Boots caught, trousers went up in white flashes, men rolled over the slick floorboards trying to smother it with their hands.

Screams layered over each other. Some were sharp and sudden, some were low and animal, cut short by the crackle. One man made it to the window and slammed it open, screaming into the night for air, and the draft fed the fire. His silhouette burned against the glass before he fell back inside.

When the fuel ran low the roar thinned to a hiss and the room fell into a smoldering, ticking quiet. The heat still pressed against his mask. The smell of burning flesh hung thick and acrid, coating the tongue. Bodies lay still in the ash and the charred stink, and the only movement was the occasional pop of cooling fat.

Elias Vane didn't notice it at first. He told himself it was exhaustion.

It started with itching. Deep, subdermal itching, like something was crawling just under the skin. He'd scratch at his forearms in the shower until they were raw, and the next morning the skin would be smooth again — too smooth. The old layer came off in sheets, pale and damp, like wet tissue paper. It didn't tear, it *sloughed*. He found a perfect handprint of his own skin in the sink, the whorls of his fingerprints still visible on the inside of the shed. Underneath, the new skin was pink, shiny, and too tight. It had no pores. It looked boiled.

Then the bones.

It happened at night, when he was alone. A deep, audible *crack* would roll up his spine, like a knuckle popping but on a massive scale. He'd wake up with his back arched and his jaw unhinged, gasping. In the bathroom mirror, his shoulders were moving wrong. His clavicles would grind and shift, the skin over them stretching thin as paper before splitting to let the bone reposition. The bones weren't breaking cleanly. They splintered, then knitted back together at odd angles. His fingers lengthened. The middle knuckles of his left hand now pointed inward, forming a claw that he couldn't straighten. He could feel the marrow turning, warm and thick, pulsing like a second heartbeat.

The pain kept him human for a while. He took ibuprofen, he prayed, he tried to hold onto the things that made him Elias — his daughter's drawings on the fridge, the promise he'd made to never drink again.

That was the last thing to go.

At first it was small. He didn't feel guilty when he lied to his wife about where he'd been. He didn't feel much when he found the cat in the hallway and his new teeth found its neck before he could stop himself. The shed skin on his hands was coming off in flakes now, revealing blackened, scaled patches underneath that caught the light wrong. His eyes had yellowed at the edges.

Moral compass doesn't snap. It erodes.

He started to like the sound the bones made. The wet *pop* as his ribcage expanded wider than it should. The way his new throat could make a low hum that made the dogs in the neighborhood whine and go silent. He stopped flinching when he saw his reflection because the thing in the mirror wasn't asking for help anymore. It was hungry, and it was learning that hunger was a better guide than conscience.

Last night he shed his face. He woke up on the floor with his old skin pooled around him like a shed snakeskin mask, his nose gone, his cheekbones now ridges of exposed bone that were slowly knitting over with cartilage. He looked at his wife sleeping in the bed beside him and felt nothing. Not love. Not fear. Just the slow, certain understanding that she was warm, and warm meant food, and food meant he could change more.

He didn't run anymore. He waited.

**Five minutes. Holding cell, Death Row. The door is already locked.**

**PRISONER:** You’re early.

**EXECUTIONER:** Protocol says fifteen minutes for final check-in. You’re the third this month. I’m trying to get home before my daughter’s bedtime.

**PRISONER:** You got a daughter?

**EXECUTIONER:** Eight. She thinks I work in “maintenance.” 

**PRISONER:** That’s kinder than the truth.

**EXECUTIONER:** I don’t think about it as truth. I think about it as a job. Warden signs the order. Doctor signs the form. I sign the log. We all just sign.

**PRISONER:** Did you read my file?

**EXECUTIONER:** I read the summary. Everyone reads the summary.

**PRISONER:** It says I killed two people. It doesn’t say I was nineteen. It doesn’t say I was high. It doesn’t say I’ve been in here twenty-three years.

**EXECUTIONER:** The summary says you’ve been quiet for the last six.

**PRISONER:** I got tired of yelling. What’s the last thing you said to the last one?

**EXECUTIONER:** Nothing. I’m supposed to say, “Are you ready?” You’re supposed to say yes or no. Then I go.

**PRISONER:** Will you ask me?

**EXECUTIONER:** Yes.

**PRISONER:** Don’t. Just… don’t look at me when you do it. I can’t stand being looked at.

**EXECUTIONER:** I won’t.

**PRISONER:** You ever think about quitting?

**EXECUTIONER:** Every night. Every morning I don’t. 

**PRISONER:** Why?

**EXECUTIONER:** Because someone else would do it. And I tell myself if I’m the one, at least I’ll be careful. At least I’ll be gentle.

**PRISONER:** That’s a lot of weight for a paycheck.

**EXECUTIONER:** It’s not the paycheck.

A pause. The intercom crackles.

**VOICE:** Five minutes.

**PRISONER:** Can I ask you one thing?

**EXECUTIONER:** You have four minutes.

**PRISONER:** When it’s over, will you tell them I was sorry? Not the people. I can’t… I can’t undo that. But for my mom. She’ll ask.

**EXECUTIONER:** I’m not allowed to talk to families.

**PRISONER:** I know. I just need to ask someone.

**EXECUTIONER:** ...Okay. I’ll tell myself you were sorry. That’s the best I can do.

**PRISONER:** Thank you.

**EXECUTIONER:** Are you ready?

**PRISONER:** No. But I am done waiting.

**EXECUTIONER:** I’ll be quick.

The lid came down with a soft, final *thunk*.

Not a slam. A settling. Wood against wood. Then darkness.

Mara pressed both palms to the lid and it didn't move. It was warm from the sun above and smelled of pine and varnish, and it was the only thing in the world. Above her, six inches of air and a sky she couldn't see. Around her, the box she was in. The coffin.

Panic hit first as heat. Her chest was already tight from the fall, from the coughing, from the way the men had lifted her out of the hole and into the box while she was still trying to explain. Now the heat was a fist.

She sucked in a breath and it was already thinner. The air inside the coffin was stale, hers and the wood's, and it didn't move. She breathed in, breathed out, breathed in again too fast and the second inhale was shallow, the third shallower. Her lungs felt like paper bags being crumpled.

*Don't think about the air. Think about moving.* She kicked. The toe of her boot hit the far end of the coffin with a dull *thud*. The wood shuddered. No give. She tried to stand and her head hit the lid. A sharp pain flared at the back of her skull and a fine spray of blood touched her lip. She tasted iron.

The darkness was complete. Not the dark of a room with a door. This was a womb and a tomb. There was no up or down, only the lid pressing on her and the floor holding her and the walls closing in on her shoulders. Her elbows brushed the sides. She could count the inches by feel. She was too big for this.

Then the sound started.

At first it was a scrape, like a shovel being dragged across stone at the edge of the grave. A pause. Then the first handful hit.

*Thump.*

It landed on the lid above her head. The wood jumped a fraction. A puff of dust fell through the cracks onto her face. She choked.

*Thump. Thump.*

Rhythmic. Indifferent. Each one a little heavier than the last, as if the man above were getting used to the weight. Dirt sifted through the seams and settled on her eyelashes, in her hair, down the collar of her shirt. The coffin groaned under it.

She pressed her face into the corner where the wood was tightest and tried to breathe through her mouth, through her nose, through anything. The air was going bad. Each exhale fogged in front of her and stayed there. She could feel her heart hammering against her ribs so hard it hurt, and then it felt too fast to be real, then it felt too slow.

*Thump. Thump thump.*

A shower now. A shovel full. It hit the lid and the lid hit her. The whole box jumped and the jolt went up her spine. She screamed, a raw, choked sound that came out as a wheeze because there wasn't enough air to make it. The scream echoed inside the wood and came back to her.

The dirt kept coming. It was a soft roar now, a shushing like a wave. She could feel the weight accumulating, tons of it, pressing down on the lid, pressing down on her chest, making it harder to draw in even the foul, used air that was left.

Her vision tunneled. The black at the edges pulled inward. Her fingertips went numb. She tried to count the thumps to stay sane. One, two, three... ten... twenty...

On thirty-seven the thumping stopped.

The sudden silence was worse. No sound at all except her own breathing, ragged and wet, and the blood pounding in her ears. The lid was covered now. The world was under her. She was under it.

She pushed up with both hands against the lid and it didn't budge. Not a millimeter. The air was a thin skin between her ribs.

And the dirt settled.

The Processing Hall smells like iron and antiseptic and old sweat. The floor is white tile, scuffed to gray at the edges where thousands of feet have shuffled across it in the same direction. Fluorescent tubes hum overhead, never off.

Mara is on the table. She is 19. Her wrists are strapped to the steel with soft-looking cuffs that are not soft at all. A screen above her head shows her file in red block letters: **UNIT 7-B / ASSIGNMENT: CONVEYOR CLASS**. She tried to scream when they brought her in but they had already put the mesh in her mouth the day before. Now the scream comes out muffled and wet.

The surgeon does not look at her. He is young, in a gray smock, his eyes on the monitor. There are three others in the room. One holds a tray of tools. One logs the time. One watches through glass.

“First incision,” the surgeon says, flat. Not to her. To the log.

The scalpel goes in just under the left clavicle. They have mapped her for this. The skin parts with a clean, surgical sound, and the pain is immediate and wrong — not a sharp thing but a deep, tearing heat that spreads up into her jaw. The anesthetic they gave her is the weak kind, enough to keep her from convulsing, not enough to keep her from feeling.

She can feel her own heartbeat hammering against the table, and then the hands inside her. They are not gentle. They peel back the muscle to expose the nerve bundle, then cauterize it. The smell hits her — burnt meat and her own blood. The monitor beeps as they thread the filament, a thin cable of black polymer, into the hollow of her bone. She knows what it is for. The others have come back with it. It is what makes them stand for 16 hours on the loading docks, what makes them lift crates until their shoulders dislocate and they keep lifting.

“Resistant tissue,” the surgeon notes. “Increase traction.”

They pull. The pain becomes a white spike behind her eyes. She tries to arch off the table and the restraints bite. Her vision tunnels. She can see the ceiling tiles, one of them water-stained. She counts them to stay. One, two, three. She thinks of her brother’s hands, of the way he used to braid her hair. She thinks of the word *home* and can’t remember what it sounded like out loud.

When they open her throat to set the vocal limiter — a small titanium plate that will let her speak only in work commands and numbers — she finally cries. Tears cut clean lines through the dried blood on her face. The technician wipes her cheek with a cold cloth, not out of kindness, but to keep the camera clear.

They are careful with the brain. That is the last thing. A burr hole behind the ear, a drill that whines. She feels the vibration in her teeth. She feels it in her soul. They insert the regulator, a pea-sized node that will smooth out fear, anger, rest. She feels the cold of it settle in, and with it a sudden, terrible quiet. The screaming inside her doesn’t stop, but it goes farther away, like it’s happening to someone else in another room.

When it is done, they do not close her properly. They staple. They stand her up. Her legs shake. The filament in her shoulder tugs every time she moves, a reminder that she is now tethered to the grid. The plate in her throat clicks when she tries to say her name.

“Mara?” the log says. The screen prints it back: **IDENTIFIER: 7-B-4429**.

She opens her mouth. The limiter lets out a flat, mechanical voice, the first words it allows: “Ready for assignment.”

She hears it come out of her own throat and does not recognize it. The pain is still there, in her chest, in her jaw, in the hollow where her nerve used to be. But underneath it is something worse — the emptiness where the person who felt that pain used to live.

They are careful with the brain. That is the last thing. A burr hole behind the ear, a drill that whines. She feels the vibration in her teeth. She feels it in her soul. They insert the regulator, a pea-sized node that will smooth out fear, anger, rest. She feels the cold of it settle in, and with it a sudden, terrible quiet. She opens her mouth. The limiter lets out a flat, mechanical voice, the first words it allows: “Ready for assignment.”

I have a color chart in my kit.

Not the one the department issues. Mine is from an art supply store, watercolor swatches stapled to a card. I carry it because crime scenes are not the gray, brown, and black I was trained to expect. They are not.

People think forensic work is about facts. It is. It’s also about light.

At first it was professionalism. You learn to see. The way a body holds the memory of a fall. The way a spray pattern maps a room like a constellation. The way a killer leaves a signature without meaning to. You train your eye to read it.

Then you start to wait for it.

My name is Mara Kline. I’m a CSI for the county. Ten years. I’m good at my job because I don’t flinch. Or I didn’t.

The apartment on 8th and Alder was different.

The call came in at 4:17 a.m. Domestic, possible overdose. By the time I got there the patrol had already taped off the stairwell and the neighbor was crying into her bathrobe. The building smelled like old cooking oil and wet laundry.

Inside, the apartment was dark except for the work lights the uniforms had set up. A studio. One room, high ceiling, south-facing windows. The owner was a painter, according to the canvases stacked against the wall. The woman was on the floor in front of the biggest one.

She was young. Maybe twenty-six. Nude. No defensive wounds on her hands. That’s what the rookie noticed first and said out loud. I didn’t answer.

She was lying on her back on a drop cloth, arms extended over her head, palms up. Her legs were bent at the knees and drawn toward her chest, feet pointed. The pose was almost classical. The kind of study you do for a reclining nude. Or a Pieta, if you were being cruel.

Someone had taken care with her.

The blood was what stopped me.

There was no mess. No arterial spray on the walls, no splatter on the cheap linoleum. Just a single, precise line of it along the left side of her torso, starting just under her breast and trailing down to her hip in a thin, dark ribbon. It had dried in a gloss. It caught the work light.

It wasn’t her blood. Her blood was inside her. I would find that later.

It was someone else’s. A small amount, carefully placed. As if it had been brushed on.

And on the canvas behind her, unfinished, the paint was wet.

The artist had been working. A large abstract, mostly ochre and bone white with a single violent stroke of cadmium red across the upper third. The red was still tacky. It matched the ribbon on her skin exactly.

I crouched. I should have put on better gloves, logged the position first. I didn’t. I just looked.

The composition was perfect. The woman’s body framed the canvas. The drop cloth was white, the floor was white, the walls were white. She was the only warm tone in the room, skin the color of porcelain, the blood line the only accent. The light from the window fell across her at a low angle, making the planes of her collarbones and ribs look like sculpture.

It was intentional. It was meant to be seen.

I took photos. I took too many photos. I took them like I was shooting art. Rule of thirds, leading lines, the way the blood caught the light at the hip. I was aware, even as I did it, that I was stealing.

In the report I wrote: Victim found supine on white canvas drop cloth, apparent ligature marks at neck, no signs of struggle, staged scene, possible sexual assault. Blood transfer pattern consistent with post-mortem manipulation.

What I didn’t write: The way her hair fanned out on the white cloth like a halo. The way the killer had wiped the floor clean around her, leaving a perfect negative space. The way the room was quiet, as if it were a gallery after hours.

The medical examiner called it strangulation. Time of death around midnight. The red on the canvas was the killer’s — a thin smear on the inside of his left cuff, under the nail. We never found him.

I still think about her. I go home and I can’t look at my own walls. I have the photos locked on an encrypted drive. Sometimes, late, I open them. Not the close-ups. The wide shots. The one where the light is just right and she looks less like a corpse and more like an offering.

My supervisor says I’m burning out. He says I’m taking too long at scenes. He’s right. I am. I linger now. I notice the way a killer arranges a body for balance. The way they use color against a wall. The way they leave a little signature in the dust, in the placement of a hand.

I tell myself I’m cataloging. I tell myself beauty is a clue.

It’s not. It’s a habit.

Last week I found myself at a grocery store staring at a tomato, thinking about how the way it split would look on a white plate. I went home and threw out my color chart.

It’s still in the trash. I haven’t taken it out.

I know what it means when a scene is beautiful. It means someone cared enough to make it so. And caring is the part I can’t stop admiring.

The noon sun was high and white over Red Creek, baking the dust until it shimmered. The tree was a cottonwood, old enough that its trunk was thick with rope burns from before.

They'd tied him with his hands bound behind the trunk. He was a rustler named Cole, thirty-something, hat gone, shirt torn open at the throat. The men who brought him didn't say much. One of them, a deputy with a sun-cracked lip, looped the noose and tossed it over the low branch. The rope was hemp, frayed.

Cole looked up once. He didn't beg. He just stared at the leaves.

"Ready?" the deputy asked.

No answer.

The rope went taut.

He dropped.

The snap was not loud. It was a wet, short crack, like a green branch breaking under weight, followed by a hollow pop deep in the throat. The sound came after the fall, a fraction late, as if the body had to catch up with what had been done to it.

His legs kicked once, hard, then went slack. The boots hit the air and thrashed, a frantic, jerky dance. The body swung in a slow arc, jerking at the end of the rope. His head lolled at an unnatural angle, the neck bent just past where it should bend.

The twitching started in the calves. Small, involuntary spasms that ran up through his thighs. His toes curled and uncurled against the empty air. The arms, tied, swung like dead weight, banging faintly against the cottonwood trunk with each slow turn. A shudder went through his chest, then another, shorter, as the last air worked its way out.

Flies came in from the mesquite, drawn by the sweat and the heat. The men stood below, smoking, not looking up for long.

The cottonwood creaked. The rope held.

The alley behind the 7th Street laundry smelled of wet concrete, garbage, and the sour tang of rust. No streetlights reached that far. Only the sodium glow from above bled down in thin strips, catching on puddles and making the brick look blacker between them.

He had been waiting three nights. Not stalking, exactly. Waiting. Hunger had hollowed him out to a thin, precise ache. It started behind the ribs and worked outward until his skin felt too tight, his teeth too long. The city noise dulled to a ringing in his ears, and every living thing that passed became a flicker of heat.

She came in alone, phone light in her hand, keys jingling. Late shift, tired. She didn't hear him move from the doorway until the air changed.

He didn't ask. He never asked.

She turned and the light caught her face. Fear flared, then froze. "Please—"

He was close enough to smell her now, salt and shampoo and the faint iron of her pulse. Hunger sharpened to a point. His jaw unhinged slightly, involuntarily, and the fangs that had been folded against his palate dropped. His throat made a sound he didn't recognize as his own.

She tried to run. The alley was a dead end.

He caught her by the wrist. Not rough, just sure. Her skin was warm under his fingers, trembling. She kicked, screamed once, a raw sound that was swallowed by the brick walls.

He pressed his mouth to the side of her neck where the pulse beat fast and shallow. The skin there was soft. He could feel her heart hammering against it, a frantic drum.

The puncture was quick. Two small, clean breaks. Pain flared in her and she arched, a gasp breaking into a choked cry. Blood was hot at first, copper-sweet, and it hit the back of his throat like fire after days of ash. The hunger didn't vanish — it focused. It pulled.

Her body went slack in his grip as the first rush took her. Her legs wobbled, knees buckling. She clawed at his shoulders, nails skimming his coat, leaving no mark. Her breathing shallowed, each inhale thin and wet. The phone clattered to the ground, light strobing uselessly against the wet asphalt.

Blood ran in a dark line down her throat, darkening the collar of her shirt, pooling in the hollow where his mouth was. The wounds didn't close. They wept. She tried to speak, but her voice was gone, reduced to a whisper that dissolved into the alley.

Her weakening was visible in stages. First the fight left her eyes, then the color drained from her cheeks. Her head lolled against his chest. Her fingers uncurled. The hammering in her neck slowed, thudded, thudded, until it was barely there under his lips. The life in her thinned to a trickle and then to a faint, stubborn pulse he could still taste.

He fed until the hollow was full enough to stand. When he pulled back, her neck was two perfect punctures, rimmed red and black, blood still beading and running. She slid down the brick, knees folding, and stayed there with her eyes half-open, reflecting the far-off light, breathing in shallow, uneven pulls that seemed to cost her everything.

He stepped back into the dark, the taste of her still hot on his tongue, the alley already settling back into silence around the body cooling on the ground.

The air in the hallway went thin.

Mara didn't see it come. She only felt the pressure change first, like the room had been exhaled in. Her ears popped. The hairs on the back of her neck rose and stayed up, each one a tiny antenna.

Then the first wound.

It wasn't a blow. A blow you can brace for. This was a *pull*. A sudden, wet tug low on her calf, as if something invisible had sunk teeth into her through her jeans. She yelped and spun, hands out, fists striking nothing but cold air. Her palm came away empty and her leg was already coming alive with a deep, hot ache.

The skin didn't look broken. That was worse. The jeans were unmarked. But she could feel the teeth — not sharp, but grinding — working. A nauseating *squirm* under the skin, like a needle being drawn sideways through muscle. She gasped, and the pain flared up the shin in white lines, then sank to a throbbing burn that made her knees lock.

She ran.

The floor was slick under her socks. She heard her own breathing, too loud, too fast, in the stairwell. The invisible thing kept pace. She could feel it when it was close: a sudden drop in temperature that raised gooseflesh across her arms, the faint smell of wet stone and rot that filled her nose and then vanished. It was always just behind her left shoulder.

It touched her again.

This time at the ribs. No impact. Just a sudden *absence* of air, and then a pressure like a thumb pressing through her shirt into the bone. She doubled over, nails digging into her own forearms, and a scream tore out of her. The pain wasn't clean. It was deep and internal, a tearing she could feel in her teeth. A cold line of agony opened between her third and fourth rib, spreading outward as if something was unspooling inside her. She coughed, tasting copper.

She slapped at the air, slamming her hands against her side as if she could swat it away. Her knuckles cracked against the wall. Pain on top of pain.

The terror wasn't the hurting. It was the not knowing where the next one would come from.

She couldn't keep her eyes still. She stared at the corners of the room, at the shadow under the door, at the empty space where her own shadow should have been, because if she looked away for a second, it would be there. It never made a sound she could track. No footsteps. No breathing. Just the sudden, impossible *presence* that made the air feel thick and then thin again.

It brushed her ankle again, just a graze this time, and she felt a cold fingertip, or a tongue, or a claw, run up the inside of her leg from knee to hip. The sensation made her skin crawl so hard she thought she would vomit. She was shaking so violently her vision blurred.

She pressed her back against the wall, arms up, waiting. The invisible weight of it hovered in the room with her. She could feel it *watching*, a focus like a weight on her spine. The worst part was the anticipation between wounds — the seconds where her muscles were coiled and her nerves were screaming, waiting for the next unseen pressure to find flesh.

When it finally took her throat, she didn't even get a breath for the scream.

The room smelled of wet stone and iron. 

Three chairs. Three friends. One empty chair for him.

The magistrate didn't raise his voice. He never did.

"You have until the bell tolls. One lives. Two die. If you choose none, all three die, and you die with them."

Mara stood in the center of the hall with her hands bound before her. The rope cut into her wrists. Behind her, the three doors were open.

In the first, Jonah sat with his knees pulled to his chest. He was 19. He had taught her how to read when the school burned. He was still missing the little finger on his left hand from the time they tried to hot-wire a truck. He was smiling at her, small and broken, because he thought it would help.

In the second, Lianne stood with her back straight. She was 32. She had carried Mara through the fever that took their mother. She had a scar along her jaw from a kitchen knife fight with a landlord. She wasn't smiling. She was mouthing something. Probably *don't*.

In the third, Tomas was on his knees. He was 27. He had laughed the loudest at her terrible jokes. He'd stolen bread for her when she was pregnant and too proud to ask. His lip was split and bleeding from where the guards had hit him earlier. He was crying, silently, his shoulders shaking.

The magistrate set a brass bell on the table. "Choose."

Mara's throat was full of dust. The air left her lungs in short, terrible hits. Her mind tried to run every equation at once.

If she chose Jonah, Lianne would live to raise a child. Lianne was strong. Lianne would survive. Jonah was young, he would only get more foolish.

If she chose Lianne, Jonah and Tomas would die. Jonah would never forgive her. She knew that look.

If she chose Tomas, he would die in fear. He would die crying. She couldn't watch him cry.

The bell was cold under her bound fingers when she reached for it. She couldn't. She couldn't touch it.

"Time is passing," the magistrate said.

Her vision tunneled. She could hear her own pulse in her ears, a roaring that drowned out the dripping water. She could smell her own sweat, sour and sharp. Every option was a murder. Every option made her the executioner they had always accused the state of being.

Jonah mouthed her name. Lianne shook her head, just once, a minute movement. Tomas looked up at her and made a wet sound in his throat.

She understood suddenly, with a clarity that made her knees give, that this was not a choice between who lived. It was a choice about who she would become. Who she would have to live with in the years after.

She could not save them. She could only pick the shape of her guilt.

Her voice came out raw. "Jonah."

No one moved. The magistrate nodded to the guard.

Jonah's smile didn't leave until the door slammed. Then it cracked. "I love you, Mara." He said it plain, like a fact.

The first shot cracked the stone. It was louder inside her skull than outside. Jonah fell forward into the chair. Blood made a dark, spreading flower across his shirt, bright at the center and black at the edges. It ran down the front of his legs and pooled on the floor. His head lolled. His eyes were open.

The smell hit her then, copper and hot.

Lianne screamed. A high, animal sound that tore out of her. Tomas made that wet noise again and then was silent.

Mara dropped to her knees on the cold floor, the rope biting deep. She pressed her forehead against the stone and vomited, but there was nothing in her stomach. Her hands were shaking so hard she thought they would break off.

The magistrate picked up the bell and rang it once. Clear and final.

She had chosen. She had killed him. The other two lived, and Jonah was dead on the floor with her blood on her hands anyway.

It started with the smell.

It was late October and the first real cold had pushed everyone inside. Mark had been in his new house on Alder Lane for three months and he still hadn’t learned Mr. Albright’s schedule. The man next door was 68, retired, kept his lawn perfect, always waved with two fingers from behind his garage door. Nice enough.

Then the power went out for six hours on a Tuesday. Mark was making coffee by the window and saw a flicker of light from the Albrights' basement window, which he’d never seen on before. The basement windows were covered with plywood. He assumed a work light.

When the power came back, the smell was there. Sweet and metallic, like old meat left in a car. It drifted through the shared fence line after a rain. Mark told himself it was the compost bin. He told himself that for a week.

The break-in was an accident. Albright had been out for his weekly walk, a little knit cap and a canvas tote. Mark’s basement laundry room backed up to the Albrights’ crawlspace access, and the connecting wall was shared. He’d heard a low thud, then scratching, and his dryer door had blown open. The shared wall panel was loose, a two-by-four pulled away from the studs where a pipe had been replaced years ago.

He shouldn’t have looked through.

It was a small gap, maybe six inches. Enough to see down a concrete stairwell lit by a single bare bulb. And at the bottom, a room.

He called it a trophy room later, because that was the word that came to him when he tried to explain it to the police. It was not a room. It was a converted storage cellar, maybe twelve by fourteen, with cinderblock walls painted white. The white was yellowed in places. There were hooks.

The first thing he saw was the wall on the left. It was lined with shadow boxes, the kind people use for sports jerseys. Each one held a woman’s earring. Not just earrings. They were mounted on black velvet with a small brass plate underneath. *L.M. - 8/14/19. M.R. - 3/02/21.* Dozens of them. Some were gold hoops, some were small studs with tiny stones. One box held a single, bloody earring, the back torn off.

The right wall was shelves. On the shelves were jars. Glass mason jars with lids, labeled in neat handwriting with a date and initials. Inside each was something preserved in cloudy liquid. A wedding ring. A molar. A small, curled lock of hair tied with thread. One jar held a pinky finger, the nail painted a chipped red. Mark’s stomach turned and he pressed his forehead against the cold wall to keep from vomiting.

In the center of the room was a table. On it was a mannequin torso, the kind used for sewing. It was covered in Polaroids, pinned to the plastic skin with thumbtacks. The photos were all the same woman, different angles, different rooms. The last ones were taken in what looked like this basement. Her eyes were open in the last one.

Behind the table, mounted on the wall like hunting trophies, were four leather jackets. Women’s jackets. Each had a name stitched into the inside collar in black thread. A fifth jacket was on a coat rack by the door, still damp.

And then he saw the freezer. An old upright freezer in the corner with the top open. It was full of plastic grocery bags. Inside one, a hand. The fingers were curled. The skin was gray.

The sound that came out of him wasn’t a scream. It was a short, choked gasp that got stuck in his throat. The bulb above buzzed. The whole room seemed to breathe out that sweet metallic smell straight into his face.

Mark pulled his head back from the gap and slammed his own basement panel shut. His hands were shaking so badly he couldn’t get the screwdriver to catch. He didn’t go upstairs. He sat on the concrete floor in the dark, back against the dryer, and waited for Albright’s car to come home.

When it did, he didn’t wave. He called 911 from his phone with the screen dimmed, and he kept one eye on the back door the entire time, listening to his neighbor take off his shoes in the kitchen next door, completely unaware that the wall between them was thin enough to hear a heartbeat.

results.model_response:
The airlock doors on Tier C had been blown from their tracks.

It started with a shout that cut through the usual prison noise — metal on metal, a shoving match spilling out of the common area — and then the lights went out for three seconds. When the emergency fluorescents kicked on, they were flickering and buzzing, throwing strobing white light over a hallway that was no longer a hallway.

Inmates poured out of the cells whose doors had been pried open with bed frames and shivs. Some were barefoot, some in bloodied boxers and stained orange, all screaming. A mattress was set on fire in the middle of the tier and it was already curling black smoke up toward the grated ceiling, making the air thick and acrid. Plastic cups and commissary trays were being thrown like shrapnel. Someone had cut the sprinkler line and water was sheeting down one wall, mixing with blood and oil to make the concrete slick.

Guards came down the stairwell in two-man teams with batons and shields, shouting through megaphones for everyone to get down. Their radios were crackling with overlapping panic.

“Code red, Code red, Tier C — we have multiple down!”

The first contact was brutal and close. An inmate swung a length of rebar wrapped in a sock, catching a correctional officer across the forearm. The baton clattered to the floor. Another inmate tackled him from behind, driving his face into the wet concrete. The guard’s shield went up, then down, and the sound of a baton striking skull was wet and flat. The officer dropped to his knees, hands to his head, blood running through his fingers.

A second officer tried to pull him back and was met with a shiv — a sharpened toothbrush handle taped with wire — that opened a line across his thigh. He went down screaming, and three men were on him instantly, kicking at his ribs and stomach while he tried to curl around his service belt. The rest of the team fired a warning shot into the ceiling, the concussion rattling the tiers, but it only fed the frenzy.

Inmates were using anything. A pipe from the plumbing. A broken chair leg. A sharpened spoon. One man had a guard pinned against the tier door by his throat, slamming his head repeatedly until the officer’s cheek split open and he went limp. Another group had dragged a guard into the dayroom and was beating him with hands, feet, and the legs of tables while others filmed it on a smuggled phone, chanting.

Guards returned fire with beanbags and pepper spray, but the spray was swallowed in the smoke and the beanbags didn’t stop the charge. The hallway was a churn of bodies, orange jumpsuits and navy uniforms tangled together, boots slipping on blood. A guard’s helmet was knocked off and kicked down the tier, rolling past a body that was still twitching.

The PA system stuttered: “All staff lock down. All staff lock down.” No one was listening. The riot siren wailed above the screaming, and the tier smelled like burnt plastic, sweat, copper, and piss.

Somewhere in the middle of it, a door slammed shut, a group broke off, and the violence moved in waves — a sudden flurry, a pause, then another rush as someone threw a chair through a window and glass rained down like sleet.

results.model_response:
The hotel room smelled like cheap cleaner and gun oil.

Mara sat on the edge of the bed in socks, a disassembled pistol spread out on a towel in front of her. She worked the bolt with a small brush in slow, practiced circles. Across from her, on the rolling chair by the window, Eli had his rifle in pieces. He was polishing the barrel with a patch, humming off-key to the static from the TV.

"Room service was terrible," Mara said.

"Yeah," Eli said. "I got the chicken. It was dry."

They both worked in silence for a minute. The air conditioner clicked.

"You did the job downtown, right?" Mara asked. "The accountant?"

"That was me." Eli didn't look up. "Took him outside his building. Clean."

Mara nodded. "Nice. I like clean."

"I like clean too," Eli said. "No mess to clean up. No witnesses to clean up. I had a guy last year who wanted a message sent. Wanted it messy. I told him I don't do messages."

"You ever do messy?" Mara asked.

"Once." He held up the patch to the light. "Client wanted fear. I gave him a little fear. It took longer to clean the hotel than it did to do the job."

Mara smiled a little. "I'm the opposite. I like fast. In and out. The less time I spend in a room with someone, the better. You get... weird. You start noticing things. What cologne they wear."

"I like watching," Eli said. "I like the wait. Sitting on a roof for three hours with a good cup of coffee. Makes it feel professional. You know?"

"Professional is boring," Mara said, setting the slide down and picking up the barrel. "I like when it's personal. Up close. You see their face. You know it's done."

Eli raised an eyebrow. "That's your favorite?"

"It's honest," she said. "No distance. No pretending it's a job."

He was quiet for a beat, then tapped the patch against his thigh. "My favorite is when they never see it coming. When they go to sleep and don't wake up. No fear. No panic. Just... off."

Mara considered that. "That's kind of sweet."

"Don't get sentimental on me," Eli said, putting a piece back together with a soft click.

"Wouldn't dream of it." She reassembled the last part of her pistol and racked it once, just to hear it. "You want the last towel?"

"Sure," he said. "I'll take the one with the stain."

They went back to cleaning.

The wood had been stacked high and dry for weeks, and it caught quickly.

At first the heat was a wall in front of her chest, dry and blistering, then a full-body pressure as the flames found their way up the pyre. It was not a single temperature but layers: the searing, bright heat from the front that turned the air shimmering and white, and the cooler, suffocating heat that wrapped around her from behind as the fire climbed. Her dress blackened at the hem and curled into ash. The skin of her forearms prickled, then burned, as if every nerve had been set alight at once. She could not step back. The stake held her in place, and the heat pressed in closer with every breath she tried to take.

The smoke came next, thick and sweet-sour with pitch and burning cloth and hair. It billowed up in a low, choking cloud that rolled over the crowd and then sank back down into the fire, catching in the throat. It was acrid, oily, and it stole the air. The first breaths burned her lungs; the later ones came shallow and wet, the smoke turning the world grey at the edges. Her eyes watered until she could see only heat-haze and movement, the faces of the watchers becoming smudges through the haze. The smell clung to everything, to her hair, to her skin, to the air behind her eyelids.

The sound came in stages. First a sharp, involuntary gasp when the flame took the sleeve. Then a low, raw keening that rose and broke as the heat climbed her arms and chest. Her voice was hoarse almost immediately, scraped raw by smoke and screaming. The final screams were not words. They were torn from her throat in ragged bursts, rising and falling with the gusts that fed the fire, then thinning as her strength thinned. The sound was drowned at the end by the roar of the pyre itself, the crackle of burning wood and the soft pop of cloth giving way.
