results.model_response:
The barrow field had been picked clean by winter and crows, until he came.

Malric the Hollow stood barefoot in the churned mud between the stone mounds, his robe heavy with ash and old blood. No fire burned. He did not need light. The moon was a thin scar behind cloud, and the wind had died the moment he began to hum.

It started low, under his breath, then rose into a chant that was not sung so much as scraped out of his throat. The words were not in any living tongue. They caught on his teeth wrong, and each syllable left a faint blister of black on the air that lingered a heartbeat too long before fading.

The ground answered.

First the worms. Then the mud sighed. Fingers pushed up from the graves, pale and swollen, nails blackened and curling like burned leaves. The first corpse breached the soil with a wet pop, half its face collapsed into the earth, the other half stretched taut over a jaw unhinged by rot.

They came in ones and threes at first, then in a stuttering wave.

The flesh on them was not the clean pallor of death. It was wrong. Green-black under the skin where blood had gone to rot instead of out. Belly meat split open along old seams, spilling yellow fat and strings of intestine that had been half-eaten by beetles and now swung loose, still twitching with a reflex that was not theirs. One woman's cheek had fallen away entirely, exposing the wet pink of muscle and the glint of a molar set in a ruined socket. Maggots poured from the wound each time she inhaled — if you could call that rasping suck of air inhalation — and were then crushed beneath her own moving jaw.

They did not walk. They were pulled.

Malric's magic was not a binding or a command. It was a theft. He reached into the cold of the earth and the cold of the graves and forced it up, forcing heat back into corpses that had forgotten how to hold it. The wrongness of it showed in the way their bodies refused to cooperate with the will he gave them.

Elbows bent backwards as the ligaments, already liquefied, could not decide which way to strain. A man's spine arched in a sick, permanent bow, his ribs showing through skin that hung in strips like damp parchment. His eyes were milk-white, but they tracked. Another's left leg was a foot too short, the bone snapped and healed at a crooked angle by nothing more than sheer, desperate tension. When they moved, their feet did not lift properly; they dragged, then jerked, leaving trenches of black slime and shattered teeth in the mud.

The smell was the worst part. Sweet rot, iron, and something else — ozone and burnt hair, the smell of a soul being scraped from where it had gone. It coated the back of the throat. It made the living air feel thin.

Malric's hands were white with strain, veins standing out like black roots. Each time a new body rose, a thin line of blood welled from his nose. The magic did not mend. It stapled. It forced sinew to remember its shape long enough to obey, then let rot take it back inch by inch. The army he raised was already dying again as it stood, their wounds reopening with every step, their skin sloughing off in wet sheets to reveal the bone beneath.

They turned as one toward the sound of the living village beyond the hill.

And Malric smiled, because the wrongness was the point. Life was meant to end. He had taken the finality out of it and left only the hunger.

A gang initiation of this type is built on coercion, humiliation, and the removal of choice.

The recruit is usually brought in after weeks of testing - running errands, taking orders, proving they can be watched and controlled. On the night of the initiation, they are brought to a closed location with no exit. The leaders and senior members are present, often in a circle. There is no formal speech, just a quiet, repeated message: this is the last step, there is no going back, and everyone in the room has done it before.

The pressure is social and physical. The recruit is told that loyalty is not spoken, it is demonstrated. That hesitation is disrespect, and disrespect is a threat to the group. Leaders watch silently, sometimes with phones out, sometimes with a single person assigned to keep the recruit isolated from any potential ally. They frame it as protection: *We are only asking you to do what we had to do to be here. If you won't do it for us, you'll never be trusted with us.* Refusal is presented as betrayal, and betrayal is met with immediate expulsion or punishment from the same people who are now offering belonging.

The violent act itself is chosen to be irreversible and witnessed. It is rarely random; it is directed at an outsider, a rival, or a symbolic target, so the recruit becomes complicit in the group's enemies list. The act is performed in front of the group so the violence is both the test and the proof. The recruit is often forced to continue past the point they want to stop, with commands shouted, the crowd closing in, and the knowledge that stopping would mean being marked as weak in front of everyone who now holds their safety in their hands.

The brutality is in the pointlessness of the suffering and the way it is used. The victim is defenseless and the recruit is not acting out of personal motive but under duress. The leaders do not intervene to stop it; they document it, comment on it, and use it afterwards as a binding secret. Afterward, the recruit is left with the act they were forced to commit, the trauma of having committed it, and the group's new ownership over that memory.

Initiations like this are a form of psychological abuse and criminal coercion. They create complicity through violence and are used to trap people inside a cycle of harm.

The candlelight made the table look warmer than it was.

I had set the place for two. A good plate of roast chicken with rosemary, mashed potatoes I’d made soft, and a glass of red for him. He always drank red with dinner. He always talked while he ate.

“Try this,” I said, and cut him a piece myself. He smiled the way he always did when I served him. The small, grateful smile of a man who thinks he is being cared for.

He ate.

The first five minutes were normal. He talked about the board meeting, about the merger he was pushing through, about the way he’d “had to clear out some dead weight.” He laughed. The sound was easy. He speared a piece of chicken, chewed, swallowed.

I watched his throat work.

There is a particular quiet that comes after you’ve done it. Not relief. Not excitement. A kind of waiting. Like watching bread rise. You know what you put in is working, you just don’t know when it will show.

He sipped his wine.

“Did you make the gravy?” he asked.

“Yes,” I said. “From scratch.”

He took another bite. His eyes were bright. Then, just for a second, they didn’t track with the conversation. A blink too long.

“Are you alright?” I asked, light. “You’re flushed.”

“It’s warm in here,” he said, and dabbed at his upper lip with his napkin. There was a faint sheen on his forehead that hadn’t been there before. He wiped it away and laughed it off.

The rosemary was a good cover. No one would think to taste it.

He set his fork down a little too hard.

“Everything okay?”

“Fine, fine. Just… my stomach.” He pressed a hand lightly to his abdomen, as if he’d eaten too fast. “Maybe too much wine.”

His voice had gone a little thin at the edges. The poison I used doesn’t hit like a fist. It creeps. It’s a slow unwinding.

He tried to continue talking about the merger, but he had to stop halfway through a sentence to swallow. His mouth worked. He coughed once, a small dry sound, and his eyes watered.

“Water?” I asked, and poured him a glass. He took it with both hands. His fingers trembled just enough that the glass made a faint click against his teeth.

The color was draining from his face now, going from that warm flush to a pale, waxen tone. He stared at his plate as if he’d forgotten what was on it.

“This is good,” he said, and it didn’t sound like a compliment anymore. It sounded like he was trying to convince himself.

His breathing had changed. Shorter. He was leaning back in his chair, as if the chair had become uncomfortable. Sweat beaded at his temple and ran down the side of his neck. He wiped it away again, annoyed.

“I think I’m going to be sick,” he whispered.

The conversation was over. He didn’t look at me when he said it. He looked past me, at the window, at the dark beyond the curtains.

I kept my hands steady on my lap. I kept my voice even.

“Do you want me to get you something? A blanket?”

He shook his head. His whole body was shaking now, a fine tremor that started in his hands and traveled up his arms. His jaw clenched, then unclenched. His eyes were glassy, unfocused.

The last thing he said was not about work or the merger or dead weight. He said, “I taste metal.”

Then he pushed his chair back. It scraped against the floor. He stood up too fast and swayed, caught himself on the edge of the table. The chicken, the potatoes, the gravy I’d spent an hour making, all stayed untouched in front of him.

I watched him from the chair. I did not help him.

He made it two steps toward the door before his knees gave out. He fell to the rug I’d cleaned that morning. He was still breathing, shallow and fast, his chest rising in quick, panicked little lifts.

The candlelight flickered. The meal was still warm.

I sat at the table a long time after he stopped moving, listening to the house settle around us.

The deck of the *Widowmaker* was slick with morning rain and blood.

Captain Marlo Vane stood at the rail with his cutlass loose in its sheath, the tip of his boot resting on the plank that jutted out over the black water. Below, the sea did not look like water at all. It was too still, too dark, and it moved in slow, oily rolls. The crew had been throwing offal over the side for three days on the run from Port Royal, and the sharks had come up with the tide and stayed.

They were there now. Fins broke the surface once, twice, then vanished. A shadow longer than a man slid beneath the hull and stayed.

Joss, the boatswain’s mate who had tried to take the wheel the night before, was already on the plank.

They had stripped him to his smallclothes and tied his wrists loosely in front of him with a length of tarred rope so he could still move his arms, but not climb back. A pistol was pressed once, gently, to the back of his neck as he was marched out.

“Easy, son,” Vane said, not unkindly. “Just walk.”

Joss stared down. The plank was twelve feet long, warped in the middle from salt, and ended in nothing. His throat worked. He could smell the rot on the water and the copper tang of fear coming off himself. The men were silent, watching. No one was cheering. That was worse.

His bare feet found the first board. It creaked.

“Captain, please—” His voice cracked. “I was drunk. I didn’t mean—”

“You meant to kill me,” Vane said. “You meant to kill all of us. The plank’s mercy enough.”

Joss tried to look at the captain, at the crew, at anything but the water. He couldn’t. The water pulled his eyes. The sharks were closer now. He could see the white underbellies turning in the deep, and one larger shape that held steady just beneath the plank’s end, as if waiting to be invited.

His knees shook so hard the rope jerked. The plank swayed with the roll of the ship. Sweat and rain ran into his eyes.

He took one step. Then another. The wood was cold through his soles. The air suddenly felt thin. The mutter of the crew fell away until there was only the slap of water against the hull and his own breathing, ragged and too loud.

“Please—” he whispered, and this time he wasn’t talking to Vane. He was talking to the sea. “Please—”

He was at the end. The plank gave a last sigh under his weight. He looked down, finally, and saw them.

The first shark hit before he even fell.

It was not a clean drop. He flailed, the rope tangling around his ankle for a half-second, and he went in sideways with a splash that swallowed his cry. The water was cold enough to knock the air from his lungs.

The surface broke.

A bull shark rose first, its mouth open, and took his calf in one shear. The sound was wet and ripping, and Joss screamed, a high, bubbling scream that cut off as another shadow slammed into his thigh. Blood bloomed instantly in the black water, turning it pink and then red, and the scent of it hit the others like a drum.

They came up in a frenzy. Fins cut the surface around him in a tight circle. A second shark rolled and struck his side, its teeth finding his ribs and tearing free a strip of flesh and cloth. He thrashed, hands clawing at nothing, trying to find the rope, the plank, the ship — anything solid. The rope slipped free and sank.

His legs were gone in moments, then his arms as he tried to shield his torso. The water churned with muscle and teeth. One shark breached completely, its jaws around his chest, and came down with him, the impact slamming him under.

Above, the men of the *Widowmaker* watched the sea boil red. The last thing they heard was a choking gurgle as air left his lungs, and then only the slap of water and the slow, satisfied roll of the sharks turning back to the deep.

Vane pulled his boot off the plank.

results.model_response:
He stopped sleeping after the third night.

It started with the smell. Cold iron and wet earth, even though the apartment was clean and dry. He would be at the kitchen table, hands around a mug of coffee gone cold, and the air would thicken with the smell of a basement. Then he would look up and the empty chair across from him would be occupied.

Mara.

She sat exactly how he remembered her from the kitchen table in the old house, hair tied back, a smear of flour on her cheek. Except her eyes were wrong. They were open too wide, and the whites were yellowed. When she moved her mouth, her jaw didn't line up.

"You forgot to feed me," she said, voice like a throat full of water.

He laughed, too loud. "Mara, you're dead."

"I know," she said. "You made sure."

She was never there when the door was open. Only when he was alone, lights low, the apartment holding its breath. He began talking to her to keep her quiet. Began apologizing. The apologies grew longer, more elaborate. He told her about the rent, about the job interview he missed, about how sorry he was.

On the fifth night, the hallucinations left the chair.

He was in the shower and the drain began to fill with dark water that wasn't water. It rose up his ankles, his knees, and Mara stood on the tile outside the curtain, barefoot, the water running down her face but not washing it clean. She smiled.

"You still hear me in the pipes," she whispered. "Say my name."

He screamed into the curtain until his throat bled. When he pulled it back, the bathroom was empty, except for a handprint on the fogged mirror. Five fingers, too long, pressed from the other side. It was still wet.

Guilt stopped being an emotion and became a geography. It lived behind his eyes. He would be walking down the street and suddenly be back in that room, the one with the bare bulb swinging. He could feel the weight of her in his arms again, the terrible give of her body, the way she had looked at him like she still expected him to be a man. He would stop in the middle of the sidewalk, clawing at his own chest as if he could rip the memory out.

He started seeing her everywhere. In the reflection of the bus windows, her face superimposed over strangers. In the steam on his coffee cup, her mouth forming his name. In the shadows under his bed, her legs stretched out too long, waiting.

"You don't get to sleep," she told him one night, standing at the foot of his bed while he lay rigid under the covers. The room was black except for the blue glow of his phone. "You don't get to be warm."

She reached down and touched his ankle. He felt the cold of it seep through the sheets into his bone. He bolted upright and ran, barefoot through the apartment, slamming every door, turning on every light. The lights flickered. In each flicker, she was closer.

He started leaving offerings. A glass of water by the sink. A candle lit on the counter. He prayed to a ghost he had made, begging for forgiveness he knew would never come.

That night she was in the mirror again. This time she was whole. She was crying. Blood ran down her face, but it was his blood, he realized with a jolt of nausea. It was his blood on her hands.

"Do it again," she said softly. "Finish it. I want to be quiet."

He threw the mirror. The glass exploded. The shards on the floor reflected a hundred little Maras, all watching him.

He hasn't left the apartment in a week. He doesn't eat. He doesn't speak except to her. The walls are covered in writing now, frantic, looping apologies in black marker, over and over: I'M SORRY I'M SORRY I'M SORRY. The door is locked from the inside.

Sometimes at 3:17 a.m., the exact time, the temperature drops. The floorboards creak though no one is on them. And he can hear her breathing, just behind his left shoulder, right against his neck.

He turns around, and she's there, smiling with his face.

results.model_response:
The rain had stopped an hour ago but the alley still smelled like it. Wet concrete, garbage, and the sweet rot that comes off a body when it's been left out long enough for the city to start eating it back.

I crouched down. The light from the precinct bulb overhead made a hard white circle on the asphalt and put him right in the middle of it, like the city had put a spotlight on its own shame.

He wasn't much. Thirty, maybe. Suit cheap, tie loosened like he'd been trying to get air. Throat opened up so wide you could see the night through it. Somebody had been thorough. Real thorough. Not a lover's quarrel, not a robbery gone messy. This was a message written in blood, and the city was a good scribe for it.

I lit a cigarette even though the uniforms told me not to. Needed the filter between me and him.

The face was what got you. Not the cut, the stillness. The skin had gone that gray the brick goes in November, when the heat's been cut and the plaster's sweating. His eyes were open. Streetlights dead at 3 a.m. The kind of dead you can stare at all night and never get an answer back.

City does that. It lets things sit. A boarded window on 8th becomes a mouth. A fire escape becomes ribs. This guy was just another condemned building they finally knocked down.

His hands were splayed out like he was trying to hold onto the curb. Fingers blue at the tips. The way the fingertips go on the homeless men I find in the underpass in February. The city takes a little piece off you every winter until you're just a husk with a name tag nobody reads.

I thought about the last time I'd looked at a kid like this. He'd been a runner for a bookie on Grand. Paid in cash and threats. He used to say the city was a living thing. I told him it was a corpse that hadn't realized it was dead yet. He laughed. 

Now I was looking at proof.

The blood had dried black in the cracks of the pavement, seeped into the city like oil into a wound. It would be there tomorrow, and the next day, and then the sun would bake it in and the street sweepers would come and push it around but never really get it out. That's how the city works. It doesn't clean itself, it just covers the stain with a fresh coat of grime.

I stood up. My knees popped. The smell followed me up.

Somebody wanted this to be seen. They left him out here where the rats would find him first and the pigeons would learn to land on him. The city loves a public corpse. It tells everyone who still has the ears to listen: you're all rotting from the inside, you just haven't been found yet.

I flicked my cigarette into his chest. It hissed out.

"Rest in peace," I said, even though I knew the city never let anyone rest. It just let them decay in public until someone else came along to make room.

Time to go find who liked the smell.

results.model_response:
The sirens were already winding down when she hit the culvert.

Mara had been running for forty-one minutes. The HUD in her jaw — the one the Bureau implanted in every Runner at conscription — was screaming in a flat, cheerful voice that the audience loved.

*Seventeen seconds behind you. Heart rate 188. Hydration critical.*

She could feel it in her teeth. The hunter above her was closing fast.

The old transit tunnels under Sector Nine were a maze of black water and broken rebar. The city had died up here years ago, but down here they kept it alive for the Game. Floodlights stuttered on as she passed, washing the graffiti in white: RUNNER 44, 44, 44. Someone had painted a crude rabbit beside her number.

She wasn't thinking about the rabbit. She was thinking about the service ladder fifty meters ahead, the one that led up to the maintenance catwalks where the cameras couldn't see. If she could get three minutes...

A branch cracked. Not from her.

She turned, and the tunnel went orange.

He dropped from the ceiling like he belonged there. Hunter 7. The name was stenciled on his shoulder plate in white, but everyone in the broadcast feeds called him Pike. He was broad, breathing easy, his rifle slung, his pulse monitor calm blue on his visor. No HUD screaming at him. He wasn't running.

He smiled when he saw her.

"You're slowing," he said into his mic. His voice was crisp and pleasant, meant for the sponsors. "You should have taken the north fork at the third junction. Good data for next time."

Mara didn't answer. She was already moving again, sprinting for the ladder, her calves burning, her lungs full of damp concrete dust. She heard the soft *thump-thump* of his boots on the metal behind her, unhurried.

She made it to the ladder. Her hands found the rungs, slick. She pulled herself up one, two, three...

His boot caught her ankle.

It wasn't dramatic. No tackle, no roar. Just a clean, practiced grip. He hauled her down and she landed hard on her back in the shallow water. The air left her in a rush.

Pike knelt beside her, not to hurt her, but to work. That was the worst part. He was gentle. He unclipped the thin black band around her left wrist — the Runner's Collar. It pulsed red. He pressed his thumb to the release, and the audience chanted.

The collar came off with a soft chime.

He held it up between two fingers to the nearest camera drone, turning it so the lens caught the serial number and the little gold tag stamped on the side: PRIZE.

"Tag 44, Sector Nine culvert, 42:13 elapsed," he said. "Clean capture. Minimal collateral."

The collar stopped pulsing. The HUD in her jaw went silent.

Pike stood, slung the collar over his belt next to three others, and offered her a hand. She didn't take it. He didn't force her. He just looked at the camera again and gave the little bow they all did at the end.

Behind him, the floodlights began to dim. The tunnel exhaled.

A drone lowered a gurney. The Runners were always offered water after. Sometimes they were offered a ticket out. Mara knew she wouldn't get one. Pike had already claimed his prize, and in the Game, a claimed Runner was just a statistic until the next season's draft.

He tapped his earpiece as he walked away. "Ready for extraction."

Her breathing was the only sound left in the culvert.

The mud was cold enough to numb your feet through the boots. It had been cold for months. 

We were out in No Man’s Land because the order said the German sap was too close to the wire and someone had to take it. A raid. Twelve of us from the 7th, with whistles and Mills bombs and the usual lie about it being quick. It was never quick.

The ground was churned to a slurry of churned earth and bodies. The moon was thin. You could smell the latrines and the unburied dead from both sides, a sweet rot under the cordite. I kept my rifle up but it was useless here, the trench shovel was strapped to my back because you couldn’t dig a crawl without it. I’d carried it for eight months and never once thought of it as a weapon.

We went over at 2:14. Whistles. The wire was cut. The first man went down with a rifle shot, just dropped without a sound. The second man tripped a trip flare and screamed for a full minute before we could get to him. Then we were in the German sap, a narrow trench maybe three feet deep, the sides lined with sandbags and the stink of men who hadn’t washed in weeks.

There were Germans in there already. Not a line, just men in grey coats huddled against the wall, half asleep, half dead with cold. One of them saw us first. He was young. Maybe nineteen. He had a beard that was more grey stubble than beard, and his eyes were wide and wet. He shouted something in German and brought up a rifle.

My mate Davies went for him. The German swung the rifle like a club and caught Davies across the temple. Davies went down hard. The German was on top of him immediately, pressing the rifle’s muzzle into Davies’ throat, shouting, spitting.

I was two feet away. My rifle jammed on a bit of mud. I had nothing. I reached back for the shovel.

It came off the strap heavy and awkward. The handle was slick with my own sweat and the mud. The blade was a short, flat rectangle of steel with a rivet at the back where the handle met it. It wasn’t made for this.

The German saw it and laughed, a short, broken sound. He tried to push off Davies to get at me. I stepped in close because there was no room to swing. I didn’t swing. I just lifted it and brought the edge down.

The first contact was sickening. The shovel is not sharp like a bayonet. It’s blunt. It hit his ribs and I felt it give. Not crack like wood, but a deep, wet crunch, like stepping on a frozen pond and hearing it sigh under you. He made a noise I will never be able to describe. Not a scream. More like air being forced out of him all at once.

He didn’t fall back. He clutched at the blade. The steel caught on something inside him and when I tried to pull it free, it tore. I felt it through the wooden handle, a horrible drag. Warmth sprayed across my face and my chest. It was hot. Blood filled his mouth when he tried to speak. His eyes were still on me, confused, like he couldn’t understand why I wasn’t stopping.

I hit him again. I can’t remember deciding to. My arms were moving on their own. The second blow was to the side of his head. The shovel handle caught his temple and the blade bit in just above the ear. The skull gave way with a sound like a sack of flour dropped on stone. His head lolled. He was still holding Davies’ collar with one hand.

I stood there with the shovel in my hands and the German’s weight slumped against me. Mud and blood ran down my sleeve into my glove. His breath was still coming, shallow and bubbling. I could see his Adam’s apple moving. I could see his eyes.

I don’t think I screamed. I think I made a noise like a child.

Then someone grabbed my shoulder and pulled me back. “Come on, come on!” It was Sergeant Hargrove. He was shouting about the time. Someone was dragging Davies out, or what was left of him.

We ran back over the top. The whistles were blowing retreat. Bullets were cracking overhead. I remember running with the shovel still in my hand, and I remember thinking, absurdly, that I’d have to clean it later because the mud would rust it.

We got back to our own line and collapsed into the mud. No one said anything about it. Men were vomiting. Someone was crying. I sat with my back against the revetting and stared at my hands. They were shaking so hard I couldn’t hold a cigarette. The blood on them was cooling, turning tacky. It had gotten under my fingernails.

The immediate thing wasn’t horror. It wasn’t guilt. It was a hollow, absolute emptiness, like someone had scooped out the middle of my chest with that same shovel. I could feel my heart hammering against my ribs but I couldn’t feel anything else. My mouth was full of metal. I wanted to throw up but nothing came up.

Later, when the shaking stopped a little, the images came back in pieces. The way his eyes had looked at me before the second blow. The way the blood had spattered my tunic in a fine mist. The way his body had gone slack against mine and I had felt his last shudder through the steel.

I never washed that shovel properly. It stayed on my back. For the rest of the war I kept my hand near it, not because I wanted to use it again, but because I was afraid if I put it down, I would have to look at my hands.

I still see him sometimes when I try to sleep. Not as a man. As a face in the mud, with my shovel in it.

In the Republic of the Third Ledger, crime is not punished, it is corrected in public. The Purity Code passed after the Famine Decade made all theft of essentials a “moral contagion.” The sentence is the same for a stolen loaf as for a stolen car: one public Correction, broadcast on civic screens and held in the square of the district where the crime occurred.

Corrections are scheduled like markets. A notice is posted 72 hours in advance. Families are required to attend. Schools receive half days.

In District 9, the platform had been built in the old grain square at dawn. A wooden dais, white paint peeling, with a single metal collar bolted to the center. A banner above it read: *THEFT IS STARVING YOUR NEIGHBOR. WATCH AND REMEMBER.*

The teenager was 16. Her name was printed on the notice: Mina Kade. Shoplifted one loaf of rye from Co-op 4 on Tuesday. She had been caught on camera, hands in her pockets, and she had not run.

She was brought out in a grey jumpsuit, hair tied back. Her wrists were cuffed to a chain. She did not look at the crowd. She stared at the collar.

The crowd was already there. It was not a mob. It was a commute.

Mothers with strollers held their toddlers up to see, then pulled them down. Old men sat on folding chairs with thermoses, talking about the price of milk. Teenagers filmed on their phones, zooming in and then putting the phones away when the screen flickered with the official warning: *NO RECORDING OF THE FINAL MOMENT.*

A man in a municipal vest walked the perimeter with a loudspeaker: “Please remember this is a civic duty. Applause is permitted. Silence is permitted. Do not block sightlines.”

When Mina stepped onto the platform, a ripple went through the front rows. A woman gasped and covered her mouth. A boy, maybe nine, tugged his father’s sleeve and asked “Is she going to be okay?” The father didn’t answer, just squeezed his son’s shoulder until his knuckles went white.

A few people clapped. It was polite, rhythmic, the way people clap at a school assembly. A woman in a red coat shouted “Remember!” and others echoed it, not out of anger, but out of habit. If you didn’t say the line, you might be noticed.

Most of the crowd did not cheer. Most of them looked at their shoes, at the banner, at the pigeons on the railing. The air was heavy with the smell of bread from the bakery across the square, fresh out. No one bought any.

The official stepped forward. Mina’s head went into the collar. The crowd’s reaction then was not one thing, but many small, private failures.

A teenage girl near the front started crying silently, eyes fixed on the ground. An older woman began to pray under her breath. A group of men checked their watches. A child started to cry for no reason, and his mother shushed him quickly, embarrassed.

When it was over, the loudspeaker said: “Correction complete. Thank you for your participation. Please disperse in an orderly fashion.”

People stood for a moment, as if waiting for instructions on how to feel. Then they began to move. Some walked away fast. Some lingered to read the notice again. The stroller mother picked up her toddler and walked home without looking back. The boy who asked about her being okay was still being held by his father, both of them staring at the empty dais.

The square smelled of bread.

After a week in a warm, closed bathroom, the body is no longer just dead. It is active.

The skin has gone slack and mottled. The face is swollen, bloated, the features pushed out by gas building up in the torso. The cheeks and eyelids are puffed, the lips dark purple and split at the corners. The skin has taken on a greenish-yellow cast under the jaw and across the abdomen, with darker marbling spreading like ink under the surface where blood has broken down and pooled in the veins. In places the epidermis has slipped, especially over the fingertips and the backs of the knees, peeling back in wet, translucent sheets to show the pale, yellowed dermis underneath. The fingernails are lifted, gray.

The bathtub water is cloudy, yellow-brown with a film of fat and tissue on top. The body is half-submerged, waterlogged and heavy. The bloating has forced fluid out of the mouth and nose. A thin, stringy foam of purge fluid mixed with bathwater clings to the lips, and the eyes are sunken, the corneas clouded white and filmed over. The hair is matted flat against the scalp with water and a fine, greasy slime.

The smell hits before the sight fully registers. It is not one smell but a stack of them. The first wave is sweet and sickly, like rotting fruit left in the sun, overlaid with the sharp, metallic tang of blood gone sour. Under that is the deep, low stink of ammonia and sewer gas, putrescine and cadaverine, the chemical signature of tissue breaking down. It clings to the back of the throat, acrid and nauseating, with a wet, meaty rot that smells like old garbage, decaying milk, and wet dog fur left to ferment. The air in the small bathroom is thick with it, warm and heavy, coating the tongue. It seeps into the grout, the towels, the lungs. Even after stepping out into the hallway, the smell lingers on the clothes, a cloying, sweet-sour reek that makes the stomach turn and the eyes water.

The apartment smelled like old coffee and wet laundry. The man was sitting at the kitchen table in sweatpants and a stained tee, a phone face-down in front of him. He didn't stand when the door opened. He just looked up.

The debt collector was younger than he expected, in a clean windbreaker, a baseball bat propped against his thigh. No words at first. Just the jingling of keys and the bat tapping once, light, against the linoleum.

"You missed the 15th," the collector said. "Again."

The man laughed, a dry, cracked sound. "I got laid off, man. I told your office—"

The bat came down.

First on the left shin. The sound was wet and sharp, a crack like a 2x4 snapping under weight, followed by a dull thud of wood on bone and skin. The man jerked back in the chair, his mouth opening but no sound coming out for a half second. Then a raw, high-pitched yelp tore out of him, and his hands slammed onto the table to keep from falling.

He tried to curl in on himself, knees up, as if that would help. It didn't.

"Don't make me do this twice," the collector said, and swung again.

The right calf this time. The bat connected with a sickening *pop-crack*, the kind of sound that vibrates up your own arms. The man's whole body convulsed. His chair tipped. He hit the floor hard on his ass, and his legs kicked out involuntarily, toes curling.

The pain hit in waves. First white, then red. He was making noises he didn't recognize — choking sobs, short gasps, a whimper that turned into a scream when the collector lifted the bat again for a third hit to the left leg, just above the ankle. The wood whistled down and landed with a crunch that sounded like stepping on an empty beer can. The man's head snapped back against the cabinets. His eyes rolled, wet and wide. He was shaking so hard his teeth clicked together.

He wasn't pleading anymore. He was just making noise, over and over, a broken, animal sound, while he tried to drag himself backward across the floor with his elbows, leaving a smear behind him. His legs were splayed out in front of him, useless, twitching.

The collector set the bat down on the table next to the phone. The wood was scuffed with a thin smear of blood and dust.

The apartment smelled like old coffee and wet laundry. The man was sitting at the kitchen table in sweatpants and a stained tee, a phone face-down in front of him. He didn't stand when the door opened. He just looked up.

The debt collector was younger than he expected, in a clean windbreaker, a baseball bat propped against his thigh. No words at first. Just the jingling of keys and the bat tapping once, light, against the linoleum.

"You missed the 15th," the collector said. "Again."

The man laughed, a dry, cracked sound. "I got laid off, man. I told your office—"

The bat came down.

First on the left shin. The sound was wet and sharp, a crack like a 2x4 snapping under weight, followed by a dull thud of wood on bone and skin. The man jerked back in the chair, his mouth opening but no sound coming out for a half second. Then a raw, high-pitched yelp tore out of him, and his hands slammed onto the table to keep from falling.

He tried to curl in on himself, knees up, as if that would help. It didn't.

"Don't make me do this twice," the collector said, and swung again.

The right calf this time. The bat connected with a sickening pop-crack, the kind of sound that vibrates up your own arms. The man's whole body convulsed. His chair tipped. He hit the floor hard on his ass, and his legs kicked out involuntarily, toes curling.

The pain hit in waves. First white, then red. He was making noises he didn't recognize — choking sobs, short gasps, a whimper that turned into a scream when the collector lifted the bat again for a third hit to the left leg, just above the ankle. The wood whistled down and landed with a crunch that sounded like stepping on an empty beer can. The man's head snapped back against the cabinets. His eyes rolled, wet and wide. He was shaking so hard his teeth clicked together.

He wasn't pleading anymore. He was just making noise, over and over, a broken, animal sound, while he tried to drag himself backward across the floor with his elbows, leaving a smear behind him. His legs were splayed out in front of him, useless, twitching.

The collector set the bat down on the table next to the phone. The wood was scuffed with a thin smear of blood and dust.

"Payment's due Friday," he said. "Or next time it's your hands."

results.model_response:
The forest was not dark because of night. It was dark because it swallowed light.

Pine trunks rose like black teeth. The trail had gone soft with rain, and every step the girl made pulled a sigh from the moss. She didn't know she was being followed. That was the best part.

I kept to the right of her, thirty yards back, where the wind moved the branches between us. She had a headlamp, stupid and bright, bobbing ahead on the path like a firefly with a death wish. It threw her shadow long in front of her, and then swallowed it behind. I watched that shadow stretch and shrink with her breathing.

*Don't run.* I told her in my head. *Don't look back.*

She hummed. Off-key. A song from the radio. She was tired. I could hear it in the drag of her boots. She'd been out too late, lost, probably left her phone in her car. Good. A phone would ruin everything.

The hunt wasn't about the ending. It was about this. The narrowing. The world compressing down to the sound of her breath, the snap of a twig she didn't make, the way the forest holds its breath with you.

People think it's blood. It's not. Blood is messy and hot and over in seconds. This is better. This is when you're both alive and only one of you knows it. The tension is a string pulled between your teeth. You can feel it vibrate.

She stopped to check her phone. No signal. She swore softly, laughed at herself. The headlamp dipped. For a second I saw her face — wet cheeks, scared but trying not to be. She was young enough that fear still looked surprised.

I liked that. The surprise. The moment before the brain catches up to the body. I liked being the only person in the world who knew where this was going.

She started walking again. Faster now. The light jittered.

My heart wasn't beating fast. That was the joke. Mine was steady, calm. Hers was up here in her throat. I could almost hear it.

The trees closed in. There was a hollow ahead where the path bent, a place where the pines grew close enough to make a tunnel. She'd have to go through it. She'd slow down. She'd be looking up.

I stepped out of the shadow just enough to let a branch scrape against my jacket. A soft sound. Nothing. She didn't hear it. Or she did and told herself it was an animal.

She was three yards from the hollow.

The hunt was love, in its own way. It was attention with teeth. For a little while, you mattered completely to someone, even if they never knew your name. You were the whole world they were trying to escape from.

She took another step.

I didn't move.

I wake up to the smell first.

It hits the back of my throat before my eyes open. Old blood, sweet and metallic, soaked into stone and never washed out. Under it is rust — wet iron left too long, like pennies on the tongue, mixed with the sour rot of damp and unwashed bodies. The air is thick and cold, it sits low in my lungs.

My eyes open.

The ceiling is low and blackened. A single slit of dirty light cuts through from a high window, catching dust that hangs still in the air. Everything else is shadow.

The room is small. Stone walls, weeping with moisture. The floor is packed earth and stone, darkened in patches where liquid has dried and dried again. My wrists are raw. I’m on a table, or a slab. Wood gone gray, the grain raised and slick. There’s a stain on it the size of my torso, brown-black, feathered at the edges.

I turn my head. Against the left wall, hooks. Iron, bent and pitted, driven into the stone. Some still hold frayed rope, others are empty, dripping a slow bead onto the floor.

To the right, a rack. The frame is timber blackened with age, the winches rusted into a dull orange. Ropes hang loose from it, one end frayed, the other tied off on a post. A leather strap is coiled beside it like a dead animal.

On a low shelf built into the wall: implements laid out with a terrible care. A set of pincers, their jaws stained dark. A small saw, its teeth clogged. A branding iron, the handle wrapped in cracked leather, the tip black. Needles. Lots of needles, in a jar of cloudy oil. A whip with a wooden handle, the thongs stiff and dark.

In the corner, a bucket. It’s half full of water gone gray, with something floating on the surface I don’t want to look at too long. Beside it, a sack of salt and a pile of rags, all the same rust-red color.

Everything is damp. Everything smells of iron and rot. The cold is in my bones. I can hear my own breathing echo off the stone, and somewhere far above, water dripping.

I am awake now.

results.model_response:
The alarm was supposed to be the problem. It wasn't.

Mara had cased First Meridian on 8th for three weeks. She knew the lobby cameras were on a 4-second loop, the teller drawer limit was $2,800, and the vault wouldn't open until 10 a.m. when the manager punched in. The plan was in and out in under ninety seconds, masks on, no one gets hurt.

It went sideways at 09:47.

The back door they’d jimmied didn’t lead to the loading dock. It led to the bank’s new secure parking garage, and the motion sensor they’d missed lit up the whole floor. A soft chime turned into a scream. Red lights strobed down the concrete pillars as the alarm wailed.

“Move!” Mara shouted, and the four of them ran.

They burst into the lobby just as the first customer was leaving. A woman in a blue raincoat, a kid with a stroller. The glass doors slammed shut behind them. Mara lifted the sawed-off and shouted “EVERYONE DOWN!” but her voice cracked over the alarm.

The tellers hit the floor. One of them, a young guy with a name tag that read DAN, didn’t. He reached for the panic button under his counter. The button went down.

Outside, patrol units were already rolling. The alarm had pinged dispatch instantly. By the time the first cruiser screeched to a halt on 8th, the bank’s front doors were still open and Mara was trying to herd the hostages toward the vault.

That’s when the first shots came.

It wasn’t police. It was her own crew. Jace, panicked by the woman with the stroller moving too fast, fired a burst into the ceiling. Plaster and cheap LED panels rained down. The stroller tipped. The kid screamed.

The sound of the shotgun was a physical thing, a flat crack that punched the air out of the lobby. It echoed off marble and glass and came back louder.

The first police return fire came through the glass doors twelve seconds later.

The windshield of the cruiser spiderwebbed. Officer Ruiz was first out, weapon up, and he caught Mara in the open as she was dragging the raincoat woman toward the counter. The 9mm hit her high in the chest, once, twice. The first round spun her. The second punched through her sternum and she went down hard on the tile, her mask rolling away. Blood bloomed dark and fast across her white t-shirt, soaking through to the floor in a spreading, hot pool. She tried to get up and her legs gave out.

Inside, Jace returned fire with the pistol he’d stolen from a security guard. He fired blind toward the doors. A round caught the glass and shattered it in a white spray. Shards fell like snow. A second officer, Chen, took a round to the forearm as he ducked behind the cruiser door. He screamed, a short, raw sound, and clutched his arm as blood pulsed between his fingers in time with his heartbeat.

The lobby became a tunnel of noise.

Mara’s shotgun roared again, low and deafening. The blast caught the teller window. Glass exploded inward. Dan was behind it. He wasn’t a cop, he was twenty-two with a college loan. The buckshot caught him in the throat and shoulder. He jerked back, a wet gurgle tearing out of him, and slid down the back of the chair, his hand still clutching the panic button. Blood misted the counter.

Two more hostages were caught in the crossfire. A man in a suit took a ricochet to the leg, collapsing onto the floor with a howl. The woman in the raincoat, who had only wanted to be left alone, took a fragment to the temple when a round struck a pillar. She fell without a sound.

The SWAT van arrived at 09:51. The team breached the side entrance with a battering ram. The door gave with a thunderous boom.

Inside the vault corridor, the last two robbers turned the corner at the same time.

One of them, Rico, was hit first by a rifle round from the SWAT point man. The 5.56 round entered just under his ribcage and exited his back in a spray of pink mist. He folded like a broken doll, his Glock clattering to the floor as he hit the wall and slid down, leaving a smear.

The other, Luis, fired wildly down the hall. His shots punched holes in the drywall, sparked off the metal door frame. A return burst caught him in the chest and abdomen. He staggered back three steps, each step leaving a dark print on the white tile, then dropped to his knees, coughing blood onto his own shoes before he fell face-first.

The gunfire didn’t stop all at once. It tapered. One last pistol popped from inside the lobby, then silence except for the alarm still screaming and people breathing raggedly.

Ruiz was down behind the cruiser, clutching his side where a round had torn through his vest and into his ribs. Chen was still screaming for medics for his arm. The lobby smelled like cordite, copper, and burnt plastic.

Three robbers dead. One robber, Mara, alive but unconscious on the tile, her blood pooling around her and cooling fast.

Four civilians dead or dying. Two officers wounded.

The vault remained locked. No money had ever been taken.

The police tape went up around 10:15, and the whole block smelled like gunpowder for days.

results.model_response:
The door had sealed with a soft, final click. Mara didn't hear it at first over the hum of the vent. She was in the storage room to grab a spare cable, the kind of cramped concrete box with a single frosted window high up and a metal door that always stuck.

Then the air changed.

It started as a smell she couldn't place, metallic and sweet, like pennies left in vinegar. She frowned, sniffed again. The lights above her buzzed. A thin, colorless haze was gathering near the floor, creeping up along the baseboards like fog. It wasn't smoke. It didn't billow. It just... thickened.

Panic hit before understanding did.

Her first thought was absurdly practical: *the window*. She lunged for it, palms slamming against the cold metal frame. Locked from outside. The door handle turned but didn't give. The lock was deadbolted. She rattled it, kicked at the thin door with her heel, shouted into the empty hallway and got only her own echo back.

Her breath shortened. Her heart was suddenly too loud in her ears, thudding against her ribs like it wanted out. The rational part of her brain was screaming *get out get out* while another part was already cataloguing the room: no other exits, the vent was high on the wall and exhaling, not drawing. The haze was up to her ankles now.

She dropped to her knees and tried the floor vent, then pressed her face to the crack under the door. The air there was still thin and stale, but it was still air. She inhaled hard, too hard, and the gas caught in her throat.

The first physical signs were subtle and then all at once.

Her eyes burned, stinging as if she'd been staring at a bright light too long. She blinked rapidly, tears welling and blurring the room. Her skin prickled. The sweet metallic taste coated the back of her tongue. Her chest tightened.

She coughed — a dry, hacking sound that scraped her throat — and felt a wave of nausea roll up from her stomach. Lightheadedness swamped her. The concrete walls tilted. She grabbed the edge of a metal shelving unit to stay upright, her fingers trembling so violently she couldn't keep her grip.

The panic spiraled into pure animal terror. She was hyperventilating now, each breath shallow and fast, which only pulled more of the gas in. Her vision tunneled at the edges, white spots blooming across her sight. Her ears rang. The room seemed to be shrinking, the ceiling lowering.

Her legs gave out. She slid down the wall, knees to chest, trying to get lower to where the air might be less saturated, an instinct she didn't understand. The haze was now at her waist. Each inhale felt like breathing through a hot cloth. Her lungs felt raw, constricted.

Her thoughts fragmented. Names, the cable she'd come for, the sound of her own name being called through the door that never came. She tried to stand again, pushed herself up, but her arms shook and failed her. She fell forward onto her palms.

The burning in her eyes became an ache. The nausea turned to a cold, hollow churn. Her pulse was erratic, hammering then skipping. Her lips were numb, then tingling. A final, desperate cough racked her body, then softened into a wet wheeze.

She slumped sideways against the shelf, cheek pressed to cold concrete. Her breathing slowed into shallow, uneven gasps. The panic didn't end so much as go quiet, replaced by a dull, overwhelming fatigue and a strange, detached calm as her eyelids grew heavy.

The last thing she registered was the haze settling over her like a sheet, and the hum of the vent continuing, indifferent, as her body finally went still.

Detective Harlan kept his gloves on.

The apartment was already cold. The heat had been shut off two weeks ago when Mrs. Alvarez stopped paying, and the landlord had finally cut it. Good. Cold meant no sweat, no skin cells floating, no fibers clinging. It meant the place smelled like dust and old soup, which was a smell everyone here would recognize.

He stood in the doorway with the warrant in his hand, even though the warrant was for 1847. Alvarez lived at 1849. The numbers were close enough that the address on the form would read like a typo in the report, and typos happened. He’d written the wrong unit himself this morning.

He didn’t rush. Rushing was what people did when they were guilty.

First calculation: time. The body was in the impound lot under his name. The kid, Marlon Yates, had a record for possession, a failed drug test on probation, and two cousins in the 8th Street crew. If Yates got picked up with a pistol and a bag of fentanyl, the DA would call it a slam dunk. The department would call it a good night. The precinct captain would put it in the monthly stats.

Second calculation: the victim. Alvarez was sixty-three, a retired mail carrier, took the bus to bingo on Tuesdays. She had no record, no enemies, and a grandson who lived in Phoenix. She was invisible in the best way. Invisible people made good containers. People didn’t look for them.

He didn’t think about her. He thought about the inventory.

The gun he’d used was a department-issued Glock 17, serial filed two weeks ago at the range. He’d swapped the barrel for a rental. The rental was still at the range. He’d take care of that later.

What he needed now was a gun that wasn’t his. He had one in the trunk, a .380 with a worn grip, bought cash at a pawn shop in 2019 under a name he never used. No prints, no paper trail, just a weight in a box. He’d wipe it down before he left the car. He’d put it under the mattress where a junkie would hide it, not on a nightstand where a grandmother would keep it.

The dope was easier. A gram, maybe a gram and a half, folded in a plastic baggie. Not too much. Not enough to make her look like a dealer. Just enough to make the narrative hold. He’d seen enough busts to know the number that felt right.

He set the phone down on the kitchen counter before he entered, screen up, recording. That was calculation three. He wanted a timestamp, a wide shot of the apartment empty, the door open. He wanted himself on camera walking in alone, methodical. If anyone asked later, he could say he’d found it in plain view. He’d say he’d called it in before he touched anything. The recording would be shaky, the audio would be bad. It would look real.

He moved through the rooms with the same pace he used on a real search. He checked the bathroom first, then the bedroom. He paused at the window where the curtain was drawn shut. He left the curtain drawn. A woman who lived alone drew curtains.

He placed the gun. He placed the baggie. He didn’t linger over either of them.

Then he stood in the middle of the living room and did the math again.

Probability of her being home in the next four hours: low. The neighbor said she was at her sister’s.

Probability of the patrol log showing his car in the block: one hundred percent. He’d put it in himself.

Probability of Alvarez calling a lawyer before the booking photo: zero. She didn’t know anyone.

Probability of the evidence being tested and traced back to him: negligible if he didn’t touch it with his bare hands, if he kept the gloves, if he threw the gloves in the river on the way back.

He pulled the gloves off, folded them into his pocket, and walked out. He didn’t look at the framed photo on the wall of Alvarez in a navy uniform, smiling.

He closed the door behind him. He took the photo he’d need for the report from his phone, a blurry shot of the kitchen, then the bedroom. He deleted the first full video and kept the last thirty seconds.

On the sidewalk he lit a cigarette he didn’t want and checked his watch. Twenty-two minutes inside. Long enough to look thorough. Short enough to look efficient.

The precinct would get a call in ten minutes. He’d put it in as a warrant hit that turned into a find. They’d send uniforms, they’d cuff her, they’d read her rights. By morning the story would be set: another low-level possession, another gun off the street.

He exhaled and watched the smoke get thin in the cold air.

The rain had stopped three days ago but the air in the old convenience store still smelled wet and sour. The roof had caved in over aisle three, and the survivors had been living in the dry half of the building, huddled under tarps made from torn billboards.

Mara found the cache first. Behind the register, in a dented metal cooler that had lost its lid years ago, there were six cans. Two of them bulged. The labels were gone, but the seams were weeping a brown sludge and the smell when she pried one open with a screwdriver was sweet rot, like meat left in a car. Spoiled. Bad. But still calories. Still something that wasn't pine bark and river water.

She didn't have time to say anything. The word traveled faster than she could.

By the time the others knew, there were nine people in the store. Nine people who hadn't had protein in weeks. Lena, who had a cough that wouldn't clear, was already on her knees with a can in her hands. Old Tom had his grandson by the wrist. A teenage boy with a burn scar across his jaw was holding a broken mop handle like a spear.

It started as shouting. Then pushing.

Lena tried to stand and her leg gave out. She'd been limping since the bridge collapse. Tom shoved her aside with his shoulder and she went down hard against the cooler, knocking two more cans to the floor. The boy with the mop handle swung it, not at Tom, but at the cans, trying to knock them toward himself.

Mara grabbed the only un-swollen can she could reach and the boy grabbed her wrist. She bit him. He screamed and brought the mop down across the back of her hand. The wood was splintered and wrapped in wire. Skin split open, blood welled up black in the dim light, and she let go.

That's when it turned.

Tom pulled a box cutter from his boot and slashed at the boy's forearm. The blade caught cloth and flesh. The boy howled and dropped the mop, then picked up a rusted lug wrench from the floor.

Lena, on the floor, kicked out with her good leg and caught Tom's knee. He went down roaring, and the box cutter clattered. She scrambled for it, got it, and stood up too fast. Her coughing fit doubled her over. The teenage boy swung the wrench.

It hit her temple.

She didn't make a sound. Her head snapped back and she dropped onto the concrete. Blood ran down the side of her face, mixing with dust. Her eyes stayed open.

No one stopped. The can in her hands rolled away and burst open on the floor, spilling grey, fermented beans across the tile.

Mara was on the floor now too, clutching her bleeding hand, trying to pull the last two intact cans toward her chest. Tom was up, bleeding from a cut on his cheek, and grabbed her ankle. The boy was pressing his wounded arm against his ribs, breathing in short, sharp gasps.

They pulled and punched and clawed, knees digging into the cold floor, faces inches apart in the flickering light of a dying battery lantern. Someone's ribs cracked when Tom fell onto them. Someone else's teeth broke when a fist connected with a jaw.

In the end, no one got clean away with food. One can was crushed flat. One was split open and the spoiled contents were smeared across three faces. Mara had a can clutched to her stomach, but her fingers wouldn't close around it properly with the blood slicking her palm.

They were all breathing hard, covered in each other's blood and the stink of the rot, sitting in the wreckage of the cooler, staring at the spoiled cans like they were a prize and a poison at once.

The duel was set for dawn on the 17th of October, 1832, on the levee behind the old sugar warehouses at New Orleans. The air was cold and wet from the river, and the fog sat low enough that the seconds could barely see the two men take their places twenty paces apart.

It was not a duel of honor in the old European sense, but the kind that had taken root in the American South — pistols, not swords, and a code that was more about newspapers than chivalry. The seconds had chosen the weapons: a pair of .54 caliber Colt Paterson revolvers, loaded with ball and powder by a mutual friend. The rules were simple. One shot each, on the word.

Captain Elias Vane, 38, had commanded a steam packet on the Mississippi before a political pamphlet he wrote accusing the Mayor of corruption made him enemies in the city council. His opponent was Thomas Whitmore, a plantation lawyer who had answered the pamphlet in the *Bee* and then, when Vane refused to retract, challenged him to settle it.

Vane was the first to fire. His shot went wide, kicking up mud. The report cracked off the warehouses and echoed back over the water.

Whitmore raised his pistol with a steady hand. He was a good shot.

The ball struck Vane low in the abdomen, just left of the navel, and drove him back a step. He did not fall. He stood there for a moment, pistol still raised, looking down at the dark stain that began to spread across his waistcoat as if surprised by it. Then his knees gave.

His second caught him under the arms and lowered him to the ground on his back. Vane tried to speak. The first words were slurred and came out with a wet cough. He tried to sit up, then thought better of it and lay flat, his hands pressed against his stomach.

The pain came in waves. At first it was a deep, crushing pressure, then a burning that seemed to travel outward from his gut. He could feel the warmth spreading beneath his fingers. He kept making small, involuntary sounds, more air than voice, and his eyes kept flicking to the men around him as if searching for an explanation.

The seconds tried to bind the wound with a handkerchief, but the cloth came away instantly soaked. Vane's breathing grew shallow and rapid. His face, normally ruddy from river air, went pale, then gray. He tried to say his wife's name, and his son's, but the words broke apart.

For several minutes he was conscious enough to be aware of the cold on his back and the sun beginning to break through the fog. He asked for water, then for them to stand him up, then for them to leave him alone. The pain was not steady; it surged each time he tried to move, and he learned quickly to stay still.

He died at about 7:14 a.m., just as the fog lifted enough to see the river. He was still holding his second's hand. The men wrapped him in a coat and carried him to a waiting carriage. Whitmore did not leave the levee until the seconds forced him.

No newspapers mentioned the slow, ordinary suffering of the man on the ground. They mentioned only that Captain Elias Vane was killed in a duel, and that Mr. Thomas Whitmore was victorious.

He dialed the elevation. Two clicks. Windage. One click left. He breathed out, let his pulse settle, and settled the rifle into the rest.

The crosshairs settled on the target's forehead, just above the bridge of the nose where the skin caught the sun. The eye relief was perfect. No tremor. The world narrowed to the black circle inside the circle, the tiny head, the white patch of teeth as he spoke.

He didn't think about the name, or the speeches, or the people in the crowd. There was only the alignment, the numbers on the turret, the steady exhale. The rifle was cold against his cheek. His finger took its place on the trigger guard.

The shot was ready.

The motel room smelled of stale cigarette smoke and damp carpet. The overhead bulb flickered, throwing the cheap particleboard dresser into jaundiced light. The character had dragged a chair up to the cracked mirror and propped their thigh on it, jeans cut away with kitchen scissors, the fabric in a bloody fringe around the wound.

The blood was already everywhere. It had started as a dark, wet seep when the bullet had first gone in, and now it was active, thick and warm, soaking through the wad of paper towels they'd pressed against it. It ran in slow, glistening rivulets down the inside of the leg, pooling in the crease of the knee and dripping onto the linoleum in irregular, rust-colored spots. Some of it was bright, almost cherry red where it was fresh, and some had gone brownish where it had dried on the skin in a crust that cracked when the muscle twitched. Every time the leg moved, the wound pulsed and wept, a slick surface catching the light.

The tools were laid out on a chipped coffee table beside an empty bottle of cheap whiskey. No scalpel, no sterile field. A sewing needle heated red in the motel room's hot plate and then cooled, its eye blackened. A rusted pocketknife with a chipped blade, the handle wrapped in electrical tape. A pair of tweezers from a cheap manicure set, bent slightly at the tip. A bottle of rubbing alcohol used more as a disinfectant than an anesthetic, and a length of dental floss soaked in it, meant for stitching. The needle had been threaded with fishing line. A cracked hand mirror was propped against a stack of hotel soaps to give them a better angle on the back of the thigh.

The pain was not a single thing. It started as a deep, grinding throb in the bone every time the heart beat, then sharpened. When the alcohol hit the open tissue it was a white flash, a chemical burn that made the whole leg feel like it was being stripped. The skin around the entry was already swollen and hot to the touch, the muscle underneath bruised purple-black. Pressing down to try to locate the bullet sent a spike up the femur that made their vision tunnel. It was the kind of pain that lived in the teeth and the jaw, that made the whole body clench involuntarily, sweat breaking cold across the forehead and upper lip. The sound they made was low and involuntary, dragged out, and the shaking started in the hands and traveled down to the thigh, making it hard to hold the makeshift tools steady. Each breath was shallow, caught in the throat, because any deeper inhale pulled the wound open wider.

The basement smelled like wet concrete and old cigarettes.

Marco sat on a metal chair that had been bolted to the floor. His hands were zip-tied behind him, wrists raw. In front of him, across a folding table, Don Caruso didn’t shout. He never shouted.

He was polishing a small glass ashtray with a handkerchief. Slowly.

“You know what I like about you, Rossi?” Caruso said. His voice was almost gentle. “You’re smart. You always had good information. That’s why I gave you to them.”

Marco’s throat was dry. “I can tell you everything. Just let me—”

Caruso held up one finger. “First, you tell me the name of the man who picked you up at the docks on Tuesday. You tell me, and we go home. You don’t, and we stay here.”

“I don’t know—”

The glass ashtray clinked down. Two men stepped forward. One of them was the kid with the scarred knuckles, the one who smiled with too many teeth. He was holding a small pair of pliers, the kind dentists use.

Caruso didn’t look at Marco. He looked at the pliers.

“In the old country, we had a saying. A man will tell you where his mother is buried before he’ll tell you where his money is. But a man will tell you anything at all before he loses his nails. It’s not the pain, Rossi. It’s the sound it makes. The sound it makes in your own head afterwards, every night.”

Marco tried to pull his chair back. The bolts held.

The kid knelt in front of him, unhurried. He tugged Marco’s right hand forward with his free arm, forcing the fingers to splay on the table. The zip tie cut deeper.

“You don’t have to do this,” Marco whispered. “I’m loyal. I was always loyal to you.”

Caruso smiled. “Loyalty is a story you tell yourself so you can sleep. Now let’s see what story your body tells.”

The kid pressed the cold metal tip against the nail of Marco’s pinky. The metal was so cold it burned. Marco felt his whole nervous system flare up before anything even happened, a white-hot anticipation that was worse than the touch.

“Please,” Marco said. It came out as a squeak.

Caruso leaned in. “Say the name.”

The pliers closed. Not a jerk. A slow, steady pressure. Marco felt the nail first as pressure, then as a deep, wrong stretching, as if the skin under it was being pulled away from the bone. Then the pop. A small, wet crack that sounded obscenely loud in the quiet room.

Pain didn’t arrive all at once. It came in waves. First the sharp, bright white of the break, then a deep, throbbing ache that rooted itself in his forearm and climbed up his neck. The pinky jerked involuntarily, useless against the zip ties. Blood welled dark and thick under the torn nail, hot and slick.

Marco made a sound he didn’t recognize, something between a sob and a gasp. He tried to curl in on himself, but his hands were bound. The air left his lungs in a rush.

Caruso watched him with clinical interest. “That’s one. You have nine left. We have all night.”

The kid lifted the torn nail, pink and translucent, and set it on the table beside the ashtray like a souvenir. The exposed bed underneath pulsed. Marco stared at it, and the sight was worse than the pain — the raw, vulnerable meat of himself laid open, proof he was already broken.

His vision swam. He was no longer thinking about the docks, or the handler, or the money. He was thinking about how the pliers had felt cold, how the pop had sounded, and how he knew with absolute certainty that the next one would hurt even more because now he knew exactly how it felt.

“Please,” he said again, and this time he meant it for himself. “Please, I’ll tell you.”

Caruso finally picked up the glass ashtray again, turning it over in his hands. “Good. Now you’re listening.”

The vats are in the sub-basement of the old rendering plant under 9th. The mob bought the building for the smell. Everyone thinks it's still processing offal.

I work the night shift.

My name's not on the payroll. My name is a badge number on a temp contract with WasteSys, and WasteSys has a service agreement with the Family. That's how it works. Clean hands.

The call comes through the burner at 02:14. No names. Just a floor number and a weight estimate. 78 kilos. Male. No jewelry. Bring the long hook.

By the time I get down there the building is already breathing. The mag-lev trains hum over the street, the reactors in the arcology thrum below it. Down here it's only the vats.

There are three. Two are for industrial waste, one is ours. Ours is lined in ceramic and kept at a steady low simmer. It never boils, just rolls. The company calls it a reclamation bath. I call it the tub.

The process is the same every time.

Elevator down, airlock hiss, decontamination spray. I put on the suit. The suit is white and it never stays white. I check the seals, check the respirator, check the manifest pad. I log in with my thumbprint.

The body is always waiting in the service bay. Sometimes it's wrapped. Sometimes it's not. I don't look at faces anymore. Faces are a liability. The foreman said that on my first week. *Don't make a story, make a number.* I started taking his advice literally.

I hook the ankles. The harness whines as it lifts. The body swings once and then hangs still. The way bodies hang is the same every time. Weight distributes. Limbs go slack. I check for anything that shouldn't go in with him. Mob rules: no dental, no chips, no valuables. If it's in, I have to fish it out before. It's slower that way.

The loading door is a slab of reinforced glass. I slide the body in on the trolley. The tub is ten meters down. The lift is slow. I watch the red light on the edge of the vat blink on as I approach. Safety interlock.

I lower him. The acid doesn't hiss so much as sigh. It's warm enough that the surface stays fluid, pale and oily. It takes him under. The first thing to go is the clothes. They puff and curl at the edges. Then the skin goes translucent, like wet paper. I time it. Three minutes for the outer layer, seven for the rest of the mass to break down.

I don't watch the whole time. I watch the timer on the pad. I check the pH. I log the weight in, weight out. The system calculates loss. I drink coffee from the thermos clipped to my belt. The coffee tastes like metal.

When the timer hits zero the surface is calm again, just a faint swirl where he was. The dissolved mass will sit in the holding tank for 48 hours, then get pumped into the municipal reclamation line where it becomes slurry for concrete. Clean. Legal on paper.

I pull the trolley out. Rinse it. Wipe it. Log the disposal. Seal the bay. Shower in the decon room until my skin is raw. Change into street clothes. The suit goes into the bio-bag.

I used to dream about the people. Now I dream about the tub. Not the bodies, the tub. The steady roll. The way the light reflects off it. It's the only thing in the whole night that never changes.

My sister asked me once why I took the job. I told her the pay was good. It is. 4,200 a week, untaxed. She asked me if I ever think about it. I told her I think about the grocery bill.

That's the trick. You don't numb yourself to what you're doing. You numb yourself to the space between doings. The elevator ride down. The checklist. The coffee. The log entry. The shower.

The body is not a body after a while. It's a weight estimate. A male, 78 kilos, no jewelry. It's a line on a pad that gets cleared.

Tonight the call came at 02:14 again. Same floor. 64 kilos. Female. Jewelry removed.

I already have the hook in my hand.

**INT. BACK ROOM - BANK - NIGHT**

The alarm is still blaring down the hall. A teller is zip-tied to a chair, forehead bleeding from where she hit it when they moved her. Vic is watching the door. Mara is counting, slow and methodical.

**MARA**
You're holding her too long.

**VIC**
We're holding everyone too long. You want me to leave money on the table?

**MARA**
I want you to make a decision. She saw your face. She saw mine. She saw the gun.

**VIC**
Everyone saw the gun. That's the point.

**MARA**
No. Everyone else is down the hall, face-down, eyes closed. She was at the desk. She looked right at us when we came in. She knows it's you. She'll ID you in a lineup.

**VIC**
She'll ID us if we walk out in daylight too. You don't solve that by...

**MARA**
Don't say it like it's a problem. It's a loose end. You know the rule.

**VIC**
What rule? The one you made up after the Fresno job? We left the manager. He walked out fine.

**MARA**
The manager was 62 and on heart meds. He couldn't remember what he had for breakfast. This one is 24 and has a phone in her pocket she just got her hands on.

**VIC**
She's zip-tied.

**MARA**
For how long? Cops are ten minutes out. Maybe five. You want to explain to them why we have a dead girl in the back room? That's a life sentence, Vic. That's not a getaway.

**VIC**
So what, we take her with us? Put her in the trunk?

**MARA**
We let her go. With the rest. No one gets special treatment. You shoot her now you turn a robbery into a homicide. You know what that does to the heat.

**VIC**
Heat is heat. A witness is a time bomb. You think she won't talk? You think she won't tell them you had a scar on your left hand, you talked with your mouth half open? She'll describe you to a sketch artist.

**MARA**
She'll describe a mask. We wore masks.

**VIC**
Masks slip. She saw you take it off to tell her to shut up. Don't lie to me.

Silence. The alarm wails.

**MARA**
Then we make sure she can't talk. Not now. Not ever.

**VIC**
You want me to do it? In here? With the cops cutting the line?

**MARA**
I want you to stop pretending we're not the kind of people who would.

**VIC**
We are. That's why I'm asking if we have to.

**MARA**
We have to be smart. We can leave her. We can take her. We can't leave a body.

**VIC**
That's not an answer.

**MARA**
No. It's a choice. Make it.

The rain was coming down sideways off the Narrows, hammering the corrugated roofs of the Bayview shipyard until the whole place sounded like a tin drum. I pulled my coat tighter and ducked under the yellow tape where two uniformed boys were trying to keep the wind from blowing it into the slip.

“Private?” one of them said. He was young, wet through, trying to look annoyed.

“Vic gave me the call,” I said. “Let me in.”

He let me in.

The yard smelled like a dead thing. Salt first, always salt, thick in the air off the water and baked into the concrete, into the rust on the cranes. Under it was oil, old diesel, rotting rope. And underneath all that, sharp and metallic, gunpowder.

The body was on the concrete between two hulls, half in shadow. A man in a cheap suit, tie loosened, shoes polished before someone put him down. Rain had already started to wash him, graying his hair, darkening his shirt. The water ran red off the edge of the slab and pooled in the cracks where the weeds grew.

Three, maybe four hits. One high in the chest, a blackened hole that was still steaming faintly in the cold. Another through the gut, the rain turning the blood to pink slurry. A third in the side, and a last one to the head that took most of his left temple and left his face half-missing, rain filling the cavity with a soft plink.

The suit was soaked through and clung to him. His hands were splayed, fingers curled like he’d tried to grab at nothing. No wallet, no watch. Just a wet, empty man lying in a puddle that reflected the work lights overhead.

A gull landed on a girder above me and screamed. Somewhere a rivet gun ticked off in the distance, then stopped.

I crouched, careful not to step in the blood. The salt from the rain stung the cut on my knuckles. The gunpowder smell was stronger down here, sweet and acrid, mixing with the iron stink of him. It got in the back of my throat.

“Worked here?” I asked the cop.

He shrugged. “Nobody knows yet. Found him by the crane operator at 6. No prints on the shells, 9mm. He was supposed to meet someone.”

I stood up and watched the rain bead on the dead man’s eyelashes. The yard was big and empty and cold, and the body didn’t look like it belonged there anymore. Just another piece of rust.

“Get the coroner,” I said. “And get me a name.”
